ideas.solution: Standard 10-20 year fixed, amortizing, assessment-pledged term loan with a construction-draw mode; underwriting from ledger feeds (delinquency, budget, reserve study, SIRS, insurance); warehouse line and insurance-company private placements; partner banks take deposits and participations. Platform earns interest on a retained slice, origination fees and servicing.
ideas.why_now: Florida full funding from Jan 1 2026 with loans allowed; Phase-2 pipeline; Vantaca now holds ledgers for 550+ management companies and 6.5M units and just launched vendor payments (Jun 2026), proving integrations are open; CondoConta shows the model works abroad.
ideas.wedge: Phase-2 repair loans in Florida, then roofs, elevators and paving nationally.
ideas.path_to_100m: Revenue is mostly interest, so count it gross: a $1.3B book at about 7.5% is about $98M plus fees, i.e. about 650 loans at $2M average, which at maturity is about 120 originations a year (WAL about 5.5 years). Against an assumed $4B/yr of national association project borrowing (Florida structural about $1B at a 40% debt share plus about $2.5-3B elsewhere; unsourced) that is about 6% share. A fee-only version needs about $3B/yr of originations and is not viable. Net interest after funding is only about $30-40M and the book needs roughly $150-200M of equity and first-loss; capital, not demand, is the constraint.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Banks: Western Alliance (Alliance Association Bank), Axos (receivables-secured 3-20 year loans), City National Bank of Florida (500+ associations), Columbia Bank ($100k+), Leader Bank, North State, American Momentum Bank, U.S. Century; public owner-loan programs (Miami-Dade, North Bay Village). No venture-backed US association lender found. Closest analog CondoConta (Brazil): about 400k condo users, over R$150M of credit, US$13.2M Series A, loans secured by receivables, integrated with condo ERPs. Risk: Vantaca partners a bank and bundles lending first.
ideas.why_they_lose: Banks sell loans to buy deposits and are gated by manager referrals and concentration limits; they hold and do not syndicate. Vantaca is software without a balance sheet.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource and switching costs (ledger access, servicing relationship, operating accounts pinned by loan covenant) plus scale economies in servicing and funding cost.
ideas.earned_secret: Association loans are bought on the deposit, not the credit: bankers are paid for deposits and the manager picks the bank. The credit is statutory (power to levy and lien), so the real risks are a failed owner vote and a project overrun, not default. No published loss rates found; verify with call-report history before believing 'near zero'.
ideas.first_90_days: Lock one Florida community bank (deposit and participation partner) and one insurer or credit fund for $25M forward flow; build ledger ingestion from Vantaca/CINC exports; get a legal opinion on pledge and lien enforceability and Florida owner-vote rules; pilot 5 loans only after the warehouse line is committed. Check state commercial-lending licensing and usury.

ideas.title: Association treasury: project-funds escrow, draw and instant-pay rail
ideas.one_liner: A custody rail for special-assessment and loan proceeds that releases money only against lien waivers and inspector sign-off, earning float and a contractor instant-pay fee.
ideas.customer: Boards with a funded repair project, owner's reps and lenders. First 10: the pilot buildings from the Capital Projects Desk and the credit idea.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Association pays a 0.3-0.5% escrow/draw fee from the project budget; contractors pay a 1-1.5% discount for instant pay; the bank partner shares float. Signer is the board treasurer.
ideas.problem: Special assessments of $8k to $300k per unit sit in operating accounts for 12-24 months; volunteers pay 30-50% deposits and release retainage by feel; the manager both controls the account and pays the contractor. Fraud and contractor-failure losses land on owners.
ideas.solution: Per-project trust account at a partner bank, dual board approval in an app, lien-waiver-gated pay applications, independent inspection, retainage rules, instant pay for verified draws, unused balance in T-bills or insured sweeps; add a reserve ladder for idle reserves.
ideas.why_now: More assessments and loans in 2026-27 under Florida's no-waiver funding and Fannie's 15% floor; Vantaca's Jun 2026 payments launch shows association payment rails are open.
ideas.wedge: Draw administration at 0.3% for the 10 pilot projects.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume $5B/yr of project flows (about 16% of the $31.1B reserve inflow, a proxy): escrow fee 0.4% = $20M; instant-pay 1.25% on 30% of draws = $19M; float on an average $2B balance at 4% with a 50% bank share = $40M; reserve ladder on $4B at 0.6% = $24M; total about $103M. Needs about 16% of project flows plus about 6% of the $63B of association deposits. Heroic, rate-sensitive, and probably not big standalone; it is a feature of the other two project ideas.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Built Technologies ($137M+ raised, owns lienwaivers.io), Rabbet, Oracle Textura, Handle, CoFi (all new-construction/lender-side); title agencies and banks running disbursements on large loans; association banks (Western Alliance with ICS/CDARS and HOA money market, Axos, American Momentum); the managers themselves.
ideas.why_they_lose: Draw software is sold to lenders and developers, not volunteer boards; banks do not ladder reserves or police contractor payments; managers are conflicted.
ideas.moat: Switching costs and counter-positioning against manager-controlled accounts; weak without the project and credit ideas.
ideas.earned_secret: The float and the fraud exposure are the same dollars, and nobody is paid to protect them (hypothesis).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign a bank trust-account partner; check escrow/disbursement-agent and money-transmission licensing and Florida construction trust-fund law (Ch. 713); run 3 pilot projects with manual lien-waiver gating.

ideas.title: Fee-only board CFO: conflict-free cost recovery for associations
ideas.one_liner: A cost-recovery service that audits insurance, reserve cash, vendors and utilities and is paid a share of verified savings by the association only, because managers, brokers and banks are structurally conflicted.
ideas.customer: Managed associations with $150k-$2M budgets. First 10: 10 boards from one friendly management company, flat-fee audit at $1,500.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The association, from professional fees; signer is the board treasurer; fee is 20% of verified first-year savings or $2-4 per unit a year.
ideas.problem: Managers hold affiliated insurance agencies, lockbox/bank arrangements, resale-document fees and vendor programs (RealManage Insurance Services exists; Florida added kickback prohibitions with criminal penalties and manager conflict disclosures in 2024). Boards are volunteers: CAI reports 91% of associations saw premium increases, 17% above 100%, 20% lost carriers; reserve cash idling at about 0.5% is a large opportunity cost.
ideas.solution: Annual audit and rebid: insurance to 30+ markets through a licensed broker-of-record partner on a flat fee (no commission to the platform), reserve ladder under an investment policy, vendor bid-leveling (landscape, pool, elevator, trash), utility and tax audits, management-contract benchmarking. Benchmark data across thousands of associations is the asset.
ideas.why_now: Florida's 2024 conflict and kickback law; hard-market renewals; reserve inflows at $31.1B a year with higher yields. Caveat: E&S property pricing began softening in 2026, which helps rebids but makes savings attribution noisy.
ideas.wedge: Insurance renewal rebid plus reserve-cash yield for 10 boards.
ideas.path_to_100m: $250k operating spend per association (my arithmetic: $93.1B / 373k) x 5% savings = $12.5k; 20% fee = $2.5k; 40,000 associations = $100M, about 10.7% of all associations or about 20% of managed associations above 50 units. Heroic, and savings attribution is hard.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Management-company programs (Associa, FirstService Residential, RealManage), brokers (Brown & Brown, Acrisure, local agents), Condo Control and Spectrum (RFP and vendor portals), CAI business partners. No fee-only venture-scale board advisor found (not proof).
ideas.why_they_lose: Managers cannot give up ancillary income; software vendors sell to managers; banks and brokers are paid on the thing being optimized.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (cannot be copied without cutting manager revenue) plus a benchmark data asset; switching costs are low.
ideas.earned_secret: The board rarely sees more than two or three insurance quotes and the manager's affiliate often holds the placement; the biggest savings are insurance renewals and idle reserve cash, not vendor rebids (hypothesis).
ideas.first_90_days: 10 flat-fee audits; two insurance renewals through a partner broker; measure realized savings against a documented baseline; legal review of Florida s. 468.4335 and insurance licensing; confirm payments come only from the association so the platform is not itself taking a kickback.

ideas.title: Manager-of-record for small and self-managed associations
ideas.one_liner: A licensed management firm that runs about 3x the associations per licensed manager through automation, priced per door-month with an SLA, for the 110-150k associations big managers decline.
ideas.customer: Self-managed or small associations (under 75-100 units); 30-40% of 373k, about 112k-149k. First 10: Florida associations of 20-60 units.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The association, from the management-fee line; signer is the board president; $12-20 per unit per month or $400-1,200 flat.
ideas.problem: A licensed manager needs a portfolio of 8-12 associations, and below about 75 doors the per-door fee does not cover their time, so volunteer boards run everything alone just as Florida and Fannie add websites, SIRS, conflict disclosures and 15% budgets.
ideas.solution: AI-assisted AP/AR, notices, violation letters, budget drafts, board packets and compliance calendar, with a licensed CAM supervising 25-40 small associations and local technicians for site work.
ideas.why_now: Compliance load jumped in 2024-26 and language models cut the routine work.
ideas.wedge: Florida small condos and HOAs.
ideas.path_to_100m: 14,000 associations x 40 units x $15 x 12 months = $100M, about 9-12% of self-managed associations. Heroic, and it resembles an AI services roll-up (a flagged cliche); weak.
ideas.who_does_it_today: PayHOA ($27.5M Series A, software for self-managed), Assembly HOA, Bluejay HOA, Vantaca (sells to management companies), CINC, Condo Control; about 9-10k management firms including Associa and FirstService (not aimed at small); thousands of small local managers; free: QuickBooks and spreadsheets.
ideas.why_they_lose: Their cost structure is licensed headcount per door; cutting headcount cuts their billing logic; regional offices cost too much for small accounts.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in staffing ratio; weak.
ideas.earned_secret: The work is license- and meeting-bound, not software-bound, so productivity accrues to whoever holds the license and the routine (hypothesis).
ideas.first_90_days: Acquire or partner for a Florida CAM firm license; sign 10 associations at SLA pricing; measure doors per licensed manager. Check state CAM licensure and unlicensed-management rules (AI cannot sign).

ideas.title: Assessment deferral: pay the association in full, collect from the owner at sale
ideas.one_liner: Pay a special assessment to the association on day one and collect from the owner at sale, refinance or death, secured by a junior lien and underwritten on the building.
ideas.customer: Unit owners, especially retirees on fixed incomes and absentee investors, in buildings with large assessments; boards benefit by being paid at once. First 10: 20-40 Florida buildings with $20k-$100k per-unit assessments.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The owner signs (the alternative is lien and foreclosure; no budget line exists, the shock creates the need). The association signs a participation agreement and needs no loan vote.
ideas.problem: About 2 in 5 Florida condo owners got a special assessment in three years (single-firm survey). Lenders will not lend into non-warrantable buildings with critical repairs; reverse mortgages need FHA-approved condos; public help is capped and income-tested (Miami-Dade up to $50k, owner-occupants, under 140% AMI, about $60M lent to about 2,100 families, $15M a round); association loans make solvent owners co-obligors for others.
ideas.solution: Funder pays the assessment to the association; owner repays on a trigger event (accruing at about 7-9%) or monthly; junior recorded lien; combined LTV cap about 50-60%; underwrite the building (SIRS, scope, reserve funding, delinquency, litigation, insurance) and the unit, not just the borrower; exclude buildings under vacate or unsafe orders.
ideas.why_now: Structural reserve funding is mandatory from Jan 1 2026; Fannie rules shrink bank appetite; a lien-based deferral is the only workable product when income-based underwriting fails.
ideas.wedge: Owner-occupied seniors in 20-40 buildings with board endorsement.
ideas.path_to_100m: Gross interest and fees on about a $900M book (about 30,000 loans at $30k, WAL about 4-5 years, about 5,000-6,500 originations a year). Against roughly 213k Florida condo owners a year facing assessments (my arithmetic from the 2-in-5 claim over three years on an assumed 1.6M condo units, unverified) that is about 3% penetration, and other states add volume. Net interest after funding is only about $30-40M and it needs about $150M of equity; capital and regulation, not demand, are the constraints.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Miami-Dade and North Bay Village programs; bank HELOC/second liens; home-equity-investment firms and HECM lenders (condo access limited, unverified); unsecured personal-loan fintechs. No private lien-secured special-assessment product found (not proof).
ideas.why_they_lose: Banks cannot price building-condition risk at the unit level and are boxed in by ability-to-repay rules; HEI firms avoid condos with big assessments; public programs are small.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (building-level underwriting data) and scale economies in servicing and ABS funding.
ideas.earned_secret: Most owners who 'cannot pay' are equity-rich and income-poor (seniors, estates) or absentee investors, not insolvent; the blocker is the building, not the borrower (hypothesis).
ideas.first_90_days: Counsel opinions on Reg Z/ATR, Florida ch. 494 mortgage licensing and any lien assignment; $2M pilot warehouse; participation agreements with 3 boards. Decisive legal premise: a junior lien on a dwelling is a mortgage for TILA/RESPA purposes and whether the funder can take the association's lien is unknown; if ability-to-repay forces income underwriting for seniors, the product dies.

ideas.title: Neutral association data exchange with an indemnified lender desk
ideas.one_liner: Managers connect once and get paid; lenders, title agents and insurers buy a verified, living eligibility record per building, and lenders can buy the determination with a repurchase indemnity.
ideas.customer: Mortgage lenders (condo project review), title and closing agents (resale, estoppel, Florida disclosure packages), insurers, servicers and investors. First 10: 5 independent mortgage lenders in Florida and California plus 5 managers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Head of secondary marketing or production operations at the lender (per-loan cost and QC line); title operations VP; paid per determination or per package.
ideas.problem: Limited Review ends Aug 3 2026, moving about 40% of mortgaged condo purchases to full review (CAI CEO, via trade press); from Jan 4 2027 the 15% test applies; $50k per-unit deductible cap since Jul 1 2026; one failed criterion makes the whole project non-warrantable. Lenders chase questionnaires from managers who owe them nothing, charge for them and answer from memory; Fannie cannot verify. Data sits in 9-10k management companies and several software systems, so no vendor can aggregate rivals.
ideas.solution: Neutral exchange with API/export connectors, a living eligibility record (reserve %, study date, delinquency, insurance and deductible, litigation, investor %, special assessments, SIRS status), automatic questionnaires, and a lender desk offering a determination with an insurer-backed repurchase indemnity; revenue share to managers.
ideas.why_now: Aug 3 2026 and Jan 4 2027 dates; 64% of boards whose building was deemed ineligible say it hurt sales or values (survey of 700+ board members, managers and partners); Florida disclosure packages.
ideas.wedge: Lender desk for Florida condo loans, then resale and disclosure packages.
ideas.path_to_100m: Lender project-review wallet about 300-375k loans x $150-300 = $45-110M (my arithmetic from NAR's 373k condo/co-op sales plus refis); resale/estoppel/disclosure vendor share about 1.5M packages x $40-80 = $60-120M (gross fee pool about $450M, mostly kept by managers; Florida caps estoppel at $299 plus $119 expedited); insurer and investor data about $40-110M. Total addressable vendor wallet about $350M, so $100M needs 25-30% of it. Heroic; a standard-setting bet, not a mid-cap one.
ideas.who_does_it_today: RealPage/HomeWiseDocs (Thoma Bravo; resale and disclosure leader), CondoCerts, Fannie's own free Condo Project Manager and PERS service, condo review vendors with unpublished prices, UWM's condo eligibility tool for brokers, InspectHOA (HOA database startup, $3.1M seed), Vantaca (system of record for 550+ companies).
ideas.why_they_lose: System-of-record vendors cannot aggregate rivals; managers profit from per-document fees; the GSEs cannot verify; HomeWise sells documents, not determinations with liability.
ideas.moat: Network economies (supply: managers connect once; demand: lenders) and counter-positioning against single-vendor records; bundling by Vantaca or RealPage is the main threat.
ideas.earned_secret: Lenders do not need perfect data; they need someone else to own the repurchase risk. Managers resist standardizing because the questionnaire fee is a profit center, so pay them to participate (hypothesis).
ideas.first_90_days: Connect 5 managers (100+ associations); run 100 determinations for 2 lenders at cost; find one admitted insurer to back the indemnity. Decisive legal premises: a repurchase indemnity may be regulated insurance (round 1 died on this), so structure it as an admitted-carrier policy with the platform as MGA; owner-level delinquency data could trigger FCRA, so keep data association-level.

verdicts.title: Tooling Bank: custody and digital twins for every OEM-owned casting pattern, triggered by foundry closures

competitors_found.name: COAST Systems
competitors_found.what_they_do: Cloud tooling management for OEMs with supplier-held tools: location, condition, maintenance history

competitors_found.name: Matix
competitors_found.what_they_do: Location tracking and documentation for molds, dies and die-casting tools at suppliers

competitors_found.name: DLA Aviation forging/casting engineering and MetaL FACT tooling database
competitors_found.what_they_do: Free tooling and supplier database for DLA-managed NSNs; located a supplier for an old backorder and saved 100-150 days

competitors_found.name: DLA/CTC/ExOne printed sand molds for obsolete castings
competitors_found.what_they_do: Cast obsolete critical parts from digital files with no physical pattern

verdicts.substitutes: Foundry-provided storage (foundry covers routine upkeep and keeps tooling in active use), OEM spreadsheets, contractual proof of ownership plus UCC filings, free DLA databases for DLA NSNs, and printed sand which makes the physical pattern optional.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Pool file's foundry count (about 1,956, 2018) is stale: 1,725 in 2022, down from 2,620 in 2003 (about 47 net closures a year). Custody at $250/set on 300k sets (8-9% of all OEM-owned sets) is heroic, because tooling in active use stays at the foundry. Closure-triggered rescue (about 45 events a year, 1,000-3,000 tools each, about 10% scanned at $2.5k) is roughly $10-25M a year. Event-limited, not a $100M path.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Illinois Tool and Die Lien Act gives a processor a possessory lien on customer patterns for unpaid balances, subordinate only to perfected Article 9 interests; a rescuer pulling patterns from an owed-money, insolvent foundry walks into that dispute. Premise that OEMs often do not know where tooling sits is supported by Casting Source. ITAR/CUI applies to defense scans.
verdicts.deciding_reason: TAM is bounded by roughly 45 foundry closures a year, foundries store tooling free, OEM tooling platforms exist, and printed sand erodes the need for patterns.

verdicts.title: Second-Source Factory: sell approved part numbers, not consulting hours

competitors_found.name: Prime in-house supplier quality teams (Lockheed, Electric Boat, Anduril, Hadrian)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Lockheed is hiring to lead PAC-3 second-source qualification; Electric Boat guides non-traditional suppliers through welding, NDT and SUBSAFE qualification
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Internal budgets; EB holds a $987M modification including SIB supplier development

competitors_found.name: DLA MetaL FACT / AFCAT and American Metalcasting Consortium (EMCS)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Free engineering support, tooling and supplier databases and ManTech-funded casting projects for DLA backorders
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: DLA-funded; AMC awarded EMCS in March 2023

competitors_found.name: BlueForge Alliance
competitors_found.what_they_do: Navy-funded supplier development and diversification for the submarine industrial base
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Sole-source contract up to $980.7M; $250-300M of the $605M supplemental routed through it

competitors_found.name: Navy Metalworking Center (Concurrent Technologies)
competitors_found.what_they_do: ONR ManTech center that helps primes and suppliers implement casting, forging and machining production methods

verdicts.substitutes: Prime SQE teams and their own approval packages, free DLA/AMC/MetaL FACT help for DLA NSNs, Navy-funded supplier development routed through BlueForge and Electric Boat, offshore sourcing agents.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $75k per approved part number is an unsupported assumption with no public benchmark. 800 approvals a year needs about 150 buyers each outsourcing 5-6 qualifications; no evidence any prime outsources. The $605M supplemental is real but only about $250-300M goes via BlueForge and none is shown to buy third-party qualification packages. Plausible ceiling is a $15-30M services business.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: DLA stat holds: castings/forgings are 3% of NSNs but 20% of the 100 oldest backorders. The part owner (usually the prime) approves new sources, often years after proof, and a GMU paper says qualification/requalification cost is why defense dropped second sourcing. Could not retrieve the DoW ManTech FY2026-2031 plan; the qualification-delay claim rests on a secondary report.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Primes own the approval gate and are hiring in-house; free government substitutes cover DLA parts; no evidence primes will buy a third-party package, which is the idea's own kill test.

verdicts.title: Tier-Three Credit: lend against the prime's payment and the customer's tooling, not the foundry's balance sheet

competitors_found.name: SAP Taulia (aerospace and defense)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Supply chain finance marketed to A&D primes with sub-tier suppliers and multi-funder liquidity
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: SAP-owned; claims $18.7B early payments for one aerospace manufacturer over 3 years

competitors_found.name: Citi defense working capital programs
competitors_found.what_they_do: PO finance, AR finance and supply chain finance for defense supply chains

competitors_found.name: Twinco Capital
competitors_found.what_they_do: Institutional purchase-order finance platform (retail-focused)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: EUR 165M package: EUR 15M Series B plus EUR 150M Santander-led securitization

competitors_found.name: Viva Capital / Cloud Capital and other PO and AR specialty lenders
competitors_found.what_they_do: PO plus AR financing for defense and aerospace sub-tier manufacturers

verdicts.substitutes: Bank ABL and factoring, PO finance, prime accelerated-payment programs for tier-1, OSC and SBA for capex, owner equity.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $100M of revenue at about 12% yield needs about $830M outstanding and a $1B+ facility; net spread is about half, so profit needs twice that. A startup lender at $250M of book in 6-7 years is generous, giving about $30M. OSC loans are capped at $150M and capex-style; the FY27 $20.2B request is mostly mandatory money the House is not matching ($2.16B loan authority); the $500M-$1B NSFF facilities are critical-minerals only, so no cheap-capital tailwind.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Financing gap is well documented (War on the Rocks, Citi). UCC 9-406 generally overrides anti-assignment clauses for accounts, but state lender licensing and true-sale treatment of PO advances need counsel. Core dependency is behavioral: primes rarely sign payment direction for sub-tier suppliers; without it this is PO finance at a worse price.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Incumbent supply chain finance and PO lenders already target this gap, the prime-sponsored structure is unproven, and the revenue test needs a roughly $830M book.

verdicts.title: Foundry BOT: build, staff, operate and transfer foundries for the new buyers who cannot hire the people

competitors_found.name: GEMCO / EC&S / J-Tec turnkey foundry engineering
competitors_found.what_they_do: Feasibility, design, project management and turnkey realization of greenfield and brownfield foundries

competitors_found.name: Inductotherm Group
competitors_found.what_they_do: Turnkey melting and pouring systems and integrated lines (e.g. WEG foundry)

competitors_found.name: In-house builders: SpaceX Bastrop, Pratt Asheville, Howmet, Safran
competitors_found.what_they_do: Design, build and run own foundries
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Pratt Asheville at least $650M; SpaceX bought about 830 acres

verdicts.substitutes: Buyers' own engineering teams, equipment vendors' turnkey packages, general contractors, hiring retired foundry managers directly.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The idea concedes net fees are 10-25% of gross design-build revenue. $100M gross is about 17% of a $3B capex pool built on an assumed 25 projects over 5 years; net is about $10-25M, lumpy, and project-based. result.pool_note: The $53.7B pool is mostly commodity castings; the defense-critical slice is small and funded through primes, BlueForge and DLA. Services and software wedges (custody, qualification, finishing, compliance) top out at $10-40M. The one $100M+ prize, turbine hot-section casting capacity, is capital-heavy and already contested by Howmet, GE and SpaceX.

verdicts.substitutes: Multi-unit owners hold their own seed rotors (DEWA rotor swap: 8 uses, up to 64 days gained, 29-day outage per Siemens). Utility groups discuss shared spares via EUCG (third-party managed, with downsides on priority and repair pedigree). OEM and ISP exchange programs give the same outage-compression benefit for a price differential. Buying parts early (OEM component quotes 12-16 weeks per PSM).

After limiting to non-LTSA, few-unit owners and 6-8 frame families, 17 outages a year is closer to 20-25% of the reachable events, over the 20% heroic line. Hot-gas-path spare sets for 150-200 MW machines were $1.5-2.5M in 2017; the $5-10M set only holds if the rotor is included. $6M revenue per outage means the pool captures 50-100% of the event spend and collides head-on with ISPs. 16-25 sets at $110-200M with no secondary market for used sets means thin lender appetite. Premise that 'nobody offers pooled sets' is partly false (rotor pools and component exchange exist); the unserved piece is a true lease with return-to-service liquidated damages.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Rotor exchange and hot-gas-path component exchange are already sold by GE, Hanwha, MD&A and EthosEnergy; the remaining lease-with-guarantee gap is thin, capital-heavy and needs 20%+ share of reachable events.

At 12-18% gross margin gross profit is $12-18M on $100M, which is thin for a risk-carrying business.
