Mixed fleets are mostly 2-3 OEMs (Caterpillar/Solar 33%, GE 32%, Bloom 14%, INNIO 11%, ProEnergy 4%), so the 'Frankenstein fleet' premise is overstated and each OEM can service its own boxes. Ownership is the money (Solaris), not the wrapper.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Air permitting risk stays with the owner. A site-level availability guarantee needs reinsurance; Cleanview warns many projects are phantom and 2027 capacity could be as low as ~5 GW. BTM may be transitional once grid interconnection arrives (ProEnergy projects expect 5-7 years of bridging).
verdicts.deciding_reason: Demand is real but addressable owners either self-operate or buy power-as-a-service that bundles O&M; OEMs and dealers cover most boxes. A pure wrapper without owned assets is a services niche with ceiling about $35M.

picks.from_title: Progressive for Turbines: a condition-priced, insurer-backed independent LTSA
picks.title: Condition-Priced Turbine Maintenance Contracts: LTSA takeout, hardware-pooled and insurer-wrapped
picks.one_liner: A 10-year per-hour maintenance contract for older-design F- and E-class frames, priced on measured wear instead of OEM fleet-average equivalent hours, backed by a pooled spare-set and core inventory and a reinsurer-backed parts-cost cap, sold through a free LTSA forensic audit.
picks.sharpened_pitch: Open with a free forensic audit of expiring or transactional-rate OEM LTSAs: normalise the equivalent-hours math, true-up, and the title-to-remaining-parts-life clause into a dollar exit value per unit. The takeout is a 10-year per-hour contract on older-design F- and E-class frames (7FA.03, 501F, 7EA, 6B) where aftermarket parts already sell 25-40% below OEM list, priced on borescope, NDE and start/trip history with an annual true-up. Do not build shops or foundries: buy repair and parts from ISPs (Hanwha Power, EthosEnergy, Allied, Sulzer, Chromalloy) under framework agreements, and own the layers they are conflicted on. First, the underwriting model and serial-level remaining-life data. Second, a pooled spare-set and core inventory financed with equipment-finance capital, which is also the hedge against casting scarcity (this folds in the spare-set pool and the core-exchange data feed). Third, a fronted, reinsurer-backed excess-of-loss on parts cost plus an outage-delay guarantee, written through a licensed carrier. Sell to the CFO and VP Generation, with the lender's independent engineer pre-cleared through a published reference framework. Keep the $100M path: 20-25 grid units at $3-4M ($70-85M), plus availability contracts on 300-500 MW of aeroderivative and behind-the-meter fleets at $80-100/kW-yr ($25-40M), plus Canada and Mexico. Raise a risk-capital facility before signing the first fixed-price contract.
picks.payer_and_signer: CFO and VP Generation at co-ops, municipal and joint-action agencies, PE-backed IPPs and industrials sign; the lender's independent engineer gates project-financed units. Budget line: LTSA or transactional maintenance fees of about $2-5M per large unit-year, plus major-outage O&M of $5-12M per hot-section event.
picks.path_to_100m: 25-35 F-class units at $3-4M a year = $75-140M, about 3-5% of a corrected ~600-800 addressable US F-class units (not the 1,100 in the original idea). Realistic 5-7 year trajectory is 15-20 units ($55-70M) plus E-class modular agreements; the last $30M comes from BTM/aeroderivative availability contracts ($80-100/kW-yr x 300-500 MW) and Canada/Mexico. Gross margin 12-18% means $12-18M gross profit at $100M, so value depends on the data and pricing edge, not volume.
picks.competitors_and_edge: Hanwha Power (PSM, https://www.psm.com/services/service-agreements), EthosEnergy, MD&A/PW Power Systems and Wood Group-lineage contracts already sell third-party F-class LTSAs; OEMs offer customizable LTSAs and can match price on the best units; Aon sells parametric forced-outage cover but not maintenance cost. Edge: no one found prices on measured condition with a reinsurer-backed parts-cost cap and pooled hardware; ISPs are parts sellers and cannot credibly underwrite their own contract; OEM averaging makes the best units overpay.
picks.why_now: The 2000-2008 F-class build-out is rolling off LTSAs; OEM bandwidth is consumed by a 116 GW backlog (GE Vernova Q2 2026) and component quotes have stretched from about 4 to 12-16 weeks (PSM); capacity prices cleared at the $325-333/MW-day cap three auctions running. Caveat: PJM's collar is only approved through 2029/30, so the window is 2026-2030.
picks.moat: Serial-level condition and remaining-life data that improves pricing with each unit; counter-positioning (OEMs cannot reprice their book without losing their cross-subsidy); 10-year contract switching costs; pooled inventory scale economics; reinsurer and fronting-carrier relationships.
picks.biggest_open_risk: Whether condition-based pricing yields a real, bankable 10-20% discount after paying aftermarket parts and repair costs, and whether any reinsurer will quote parts-cost excess-of-loss when standard property cover excludes wear and tear; secondarily OEM price-matching on the best units and casting scarcity hitting independents harder than OEMs.
picks.cheapest_next_test: Six weeks, under $25k: run five free LTSA forensic reviews for co-ops and municipal agencies, price each unit on its borescope/NDE and operating history versus the OEM equivalent-hours quote, ask two specialty reinsurers through a broker for an indicative parts-cost excess-of-loss term sheet, and interview three lender independent engineers. Kill if the median measured saving is below about 8% or no reinsurer will quote.

result.pool_note: Big pool, but value flows through OEM lock-in and PE or conglomerate-backed ISPs that already run rotor, component and LTSA programs. Most gaps were existing ISP offers or thin staffing and brokerage layers. Only the pricing-and-risk wrapper on independent LTSAs stayed large and unproductised, with a realistic ceiling near $70M.

ideas.title: Pre-Op Lock: ancillary network check at prior authorization
ideas.one_liner: Catch the 20x-QPA awards weeks before the surgery: at prior authorization, find the out-of-network ancillary vendor a surgeon always uses and lock an in-network rate or reroute the case.
ideas.customer: Mid-size TPAs and regional Blues (and the self-funded sponsors behind them) with heavy neuro and surgery IDR exposure. First 10: ten TPAs/regional payers with 100k-1M lives in TX, FL, AZ, TN, NY, CA (top states by line items per PayerPrice).
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Network Management or Chief Medical Officer (UM) at the TPA/payer; for carve-outs the sponsor's benefits director. Budget line: cost containment / UM vendor fees. Price (A): 12-15% of verified avoided award dollars, floor about $25 per scheduled-procedure authorization.
ideas.problem: The ER is the headline but scheduled care carries the multiples. (S) Neuro/neuromuscular is about 14% of H2 2025 determinations (~160k) at 19-24x QPA; surgery 13.6x; breast reconstruction 32x; surgery awards alone $3.8B in 2023-25. (A) With medians as proxies and equal QPA per line, neuro dollars are about 2x ED dollars on a quarter of the count. (U) The neuro category is probably mostly intraoperative neuromonitoring and similar add-ons; sources do not break it out. These are ancillaries at in-network facilities; the plan sees the case weeks ahead via prior auth, but nobody checks the ancillary's network status then.
ideas.solution: Pre-service layer on the prior-auth feed (X12 278 / UM portal) plus 24-36 months of claims: learn the (surgeon, facility) to ancillary-vendor map, flag out-of-network vendors, then (1) open a single-case agreement at a benchmark-linked rate before surgery, (2) attach an authorization condition and name in-network vendors to the surgeon, (3) reroute to a facility whose usual ancillaries are in-network, (4) keep an ERISA prudence file. Revenue is a share of avoided awards.
ideas.why_now: 2025 data exposed 20-30x outliers; the NYT $440,000 breast-reduction story (Apr 2026) and ERIC's Sep 2026 interviews moved sponsors; $15 filings make every residual ancillary claim worth disputing; the Ops Rule portal gives sponsors visibility.
ideas.wedge: Spine and neuro procedures with intraoperative monitoring, plus assistant surgeons, at three TPAs in TX, FL and AZ; outcome measured against a matched control of authorizations.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Scheduled-procedure ancillary awards (neuro + surgery + plastics) assumed at 30% of $15B = $4.5B in 2025, about $6-7B in 2026E. At 12% of avoided dollars, $100M needs about $830M avoided a year = 12-14% of the category (28% if only half is avoidable). Heroic share, but the lever is the payer's own authorization; two of the top four payers (about 75% of determined line items) or ~20 mid-size TPAs would carry it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Payer network teams negotiating single-case agreements by hand; UM vendors paid per review (eviCore, Carelon; U); provider-side prior-auth automation (Cohere Health); post-service repricing (Zelis, Claritev); IONM vendors contracting with facilities (e.g. NuVasive Clinical Services). I found no vendor selling an ancillary-network check at authorization; a search for IONM-specific IDR strategy returned only payer coverage policies.
ideas.why_they_lose: UM vendors are paid per review and judged on medical necessity; network teams are judged on in-network rate, not dispute exposure; Zelis/Claritev engage after the claim exists; provider-facing prior-auth tools serve the provider.
ideas.moat: Process power and switching costs (embedded in the authorization workflow); pooled facility x surgeon x vendor map across payers is a data network effect; counter-positioning against per-review vendors.
ideas.earned_secret: The ER is unpredictable; the 2,450% awards are the opposite. The ancillary vendor is set by the surgeon's habit and is visible two to six weeks ahead, and one claims-history lookup predicts it. Legal premise to check: whether intraoperative monitoring counts as an NSA ancillary, ERISA/state UM limits on conditioning authorization, HIPAA business-associate terms.
ideas.first_90_days: Pull 24 months of claims from 2-3 TPAs; build the vendor map for the top 100 spine/neuro surgeons per metro; produce a forward 90-day exposure list; negotiate 10 single-case agreements; measure avoided award vs matched control; hire a former payer network contractor and an IONM billing lead.

ideas.title: Sponsor Desk: the employer's own IDR control tower
ideas.one_liner: Give the employer that actually pays every award a control tower and a written authority grid its TPA must follow, priced flat per member, because contingency representation fails on the math.
ideas.customer: Self-funded sponsors with 1,000+ lives; public plans and Taft-Hartley funds first, mid-market through brokers later. First 10: City of San Antonio plan, NY Empire Plan, 32BJ Health Fund, 1199SEIU Funds, Teachers Health Trust, plus five ERIC-member employers; all have disclosed IDR losses publicly.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Plan fiduciary committee: VP Total Rewards or CFO; for funds, trustees and fund administrator. Budget: plan administrative expense paid from plan assets, next to the TPA fee. The Ops Rule says delegating to a TPA does not relieve the sponsor and gives each self-funded plan its own registry number and portal visibility.
ideas.problem: TPAs run IDR as a billed-back cost centre (Premera: $2,500 management fee plus pass-through) with no performance standard; sponsors cannot see which provider groups drive exposure; in practice no one at the TPA holds written offer, entity-strike or settlement authority from the sponsor, so staff take the safe default. Exposure is concentrated: one chain's four ERs were 53% of San Antonio's ED claims cost at a 99.6% provider win rate. One sponsor found QPA+10% offers 'functionally random'.
ideas.solution: Ingest TPA IDR reports, portal notices and claims; show exposure by provider group, entity, specialty and trend; flag defaults and ineligible filings; push an authority grid (offer bands, entity strike list, settlement bands, direct-contract triggers) to the TPA as plan instructions; fiduciary-grade reporting; hand targeted cases to Pre-Op Lock, Lockstep, Cold Open and Plumb Line. Flat fee of about $3-6 per member per year (A), no savings share.
ideas.why_now: ERIC's Sep 22 2026 white paper; Marketplace (Oct 9 2026); CBO's June 2026 call for research; registry/portal rollout; 2027 renewals. Sponsors told ERIC they cannot reliably determine what IDR costs them.
ideas.wedge: Free 30-day audit of the sponsor's last 24 months of IDR determinations, built from the TPA's own reports.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) About 100M self-funded lives (154M with employer coverage x 67%). At $5 per life per year that is 20M lives (20%); with Pre-Op Lock, Lockstep and Plumb Line modules lifting revenue to ~$12 per life it is 8.3M lives (8%). IDR cost per self-funded life was ~$100-135 in 2025 ($15B x 65-90% / 100M), so $5 is under 5% of spend.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Payer/TPA-side: Zelis NSA Claim Advantage, Claritev IDR services, Daffodil's AI tool. Provider-side: PayerPrice, HaloMD, Pivotal Health. Consultants (Aon, Hub) publish checklists but sell no tool; unnamed contingency representatives pitch sponsors; TPAs' own IDR reports. I found no sponsor-side software.
ideas.why_they_lose: TPAs and carriers earn per-case fees and cannot grade themselves; Zelis and Claritev sell to TPAs, so an adversarial sponsor tool conflicts with their channel; brokers/consultants are paid by carriers (U) and sell advice; contingency fees consume the savings (ERIC sponsor).
ideas.moat: Switching costs (policy engine plus plan-level registry identity); a cross-TPA record, because sponsors use several carriers and no single TPA can bundle it; pooled entity-outcome data that no public file has (entity names are not in the CMS file).
ideas.earned_secret: The offer number is not the lever. Contested provider win rate is flat near 86%, defaults (22% of determinations) are less provider-friendly (59-75%) than contests, and entity dispersion runs 19%-99%. The levers are concentration, entity choice, eligibility, and the sponsor's written authority, which nobody has ever issued. Legal premise to check: HIPAA access as the plan's business associate; ASO terms on sponsor-directed offers; (U) Texas HB 1592 opt-in for self-funded plans.
ideas.first_90_days: Obtain IDR reports from 5 sponsors; build the provider-concentration view; sign 3 paid pilots; draft an ASO addendum with ERISA counsel; get registry-ready.

ideas.title: Lockstep: employer master agreements with the ten big filers
ideas.one_liner: A multi-employer buying coalition that signs rate-card master agreements with the groups filing two-thirds of all disputes, so the plan pays a fair collared price in seven days instead of rolling dice at 404% of QPA 150 days later (PBM-style benefit manager on a pass-through flow).
ideas.customer: Public plans, Taft-Hartley funds and large self-funded employers acting through their TPAs; counterparties are the top-10 filers (66-69% of 2025 filings). First 10: the five public/union plans above plus five large employers; start with radiology (Radiology Partners files nearly all radiology disputes) and ED.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The sponsor (VP Total Rewards/CFO/trustees) from its claims budget; Lockstep takes 10-12% of verified savings against an expected-IDR counterfactual plus a fast-pay spread shared with Float. The group's CEO/CFO signs the master agreement.
ideas.problem: A zone of agreement exists but nobody can reach it. (A) A provider nets ~280% of QPA from a 404% award after a 20% intermediary share, ~4% cost of waiting 100-150 days and ~10% nonpayment/underpayment risk (EDPMA: 24% unpaid or incorrect at 30 days). The plan's all-in cost of that award is 404% plus ~$857 internal cost plus its entity-fee share. A contract at 260-300% with seven-day pay beats both. Carriers cannot offer it (an above-QPA payment sets a floor that feeds the statutory contract-history factor and their network pricing; ASO schedules earn fees on disputes) and single employers cannot judge quotes ('far above market', ERIC).
ideas.solution: Sponsor coalition negotiating via a messenger model; master agreement with a rate card by specialty and market indexed to the QPA-of-record with a collar, three-year term, non-precedent clause and a regime-change clause that swaps the index if a benchmark law passes; plan opt-in by instruction to the TPA with claims routed at adjudication; seven-day pay via Float; annual reconciliation and a prudence file.
ideas.why_now: Employers are loud (ERIC, Marketplace); TeamHealth says it would prefer to be in network at fair rates and has approached ~15 employers; Pallone's 2028 date gives groups a reason to lock multi-year rates now; TMA III will raise QPAs and compress the award-to-QPA ratio.
ideas.wedge: Radiology plus ED for the five public/union plans; Teachers Health Trust is the existence proof (direct TeamHealth deal in weeks, $500k saved in fees alone).
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Self-funded award dollars were $9.8-13.5B in 2025 (65-90% of $15B) and perhaps $13-20B in 2026 if H1 volume growth (+50%) holds. Savings of 30% on converted flow at an 11% take means $100M needs $3.0B converted = 15-23% of self-funded flow. Heroic share; concentration helps because ~ten counterparties cover two-thirds of filings.
ideas.who_does_it_today: TeamHealth direct deals one employer at a time; Tribunus Health (negotiation firm quoted by HFMA); open-negotiation modules in Zelis, Claritev (400k post-payment disputes negotiated in 2025, company-reported) and Daffodil; employers alone. No multi-employer neutral coalition found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Carriers: precedent and ASO fee income. Zelis/Claritev/Daffodil: paid by payers per claim or on savings and cannot be adversarial to TPA customers. HaloMD: its fee is a share of the award, so settling at 270% cuts its income. TeamHealth alone: no benchmark credibility, no pooled volume.
ideas.moat: Network economies (employer volume attracts group acceptance and vice versa), counter-positioning against fee-on-dispute models, and scale in negotiation.
ideas.earned_secret: (ED/radiology revenue-cycle director) The groups do not want to arbitrate either: net of intermediary cut, delay and nonpayment a 404% award is worth ~280% to them. What they cannot do is quote a number that becomes the national floor; a coalition with a neutral benchmark gives them cover. Legal premise to check: antitrust (buyer coalition, no boycott), treatment of settlements under the previous-contracted-rates factor, ERISA prudence for above-QPA rates.
ideas.first_90_days: Letters of intent from the five public/union plans (~1.5-2M lives, A); antitrust counsel on the messenger model; ERISA counsel on prudence; one pilot rate card with one national group; build the index with Plumb Line.

ideas.title: Float: seven-day pay against contract-rate receivables
ideas.one_liner: Pay the group in seven days at a known discount, funded against contract-rate claims a plan has agreed to pay and awards from payers that reliably pay, with remittance flowing through a lockbox the funder controls (float and spread on a payment rail; legal-shock claims pool).
ideas.customer: Hospital-based physician groups signed to Lockstep or Cold Open agreements; independent anesthesia, radiology and EM groups first. First 10: ten independent groups with $2-10M of open awards (Becker's cites a group carrying $2.1M unpaid).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Group CFO/practice administrator from the working-capital line; discount 1.5-3% (A). The plan authorizes the lockbox as part of the master agreement.
ideas.problem: Cash arrives 100-150+ days after service; the 30-day award deadline is routinely missed (EDPMA 24% unpaid or incorrect); there is no private right of action to enforce awards (Fifth Circuit, cert denied Jan 2026) and CMS complaints recovered ~$30M in four years, so lending against a bare award is fragile.
ideas.solution: (1) Contract-rate claims under Lockstep/Cold Open: pay at seven days; the plan funds the lockbox on a 30-day schedule, enforceable as an ordinary contract. (2) Determined awards: score by payer x entity x eligibility cleanliness, buy only from payers with a good payment record, take assignment of proceeds, price for lateness, decline awards with eligibility defects. (3) Fund with a warehouse line, later ABS.
ideas.why_now: Lockstep creates contract receivables that did not exist; independent groups are cash-strained; the Fifth Circuit ruling pushed risk onto whoever holds the paper.
ideas.wedge: Fast-pay for the first Lockstep deals, then determined awards from the three best-paying payers for ten independent groups.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) $5B of annual volume x 2% = $100M; ~50 days outstanding means ~$685M of capital. Volume: $2B of Lockstep contract flow plus $3B of independent groups' determined awards (about half of an assumed $6-7B in 2026E). Heroic without Lockstep.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No source found on financing IDR awards. Hidden incumbents: medical-receivables lenders and factors (U), PE-backed groups self-funding, Zelis Payments on the payer rail.
ideas.why_they_lose: Zelis is paid by payers and early pay erodes payer float; intermediaries are paid on the award, not on speed; banks do not understand the collateral.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in funding cost plus a proprietary payer-payment-behavior dataset (cornered resource).
ideas.earned_secret: The risk is lateness and mis-payment, not default; priced correctly, lateness is the revenue. Weakest legal premise in the set: validity of assignment of proceeds, true-sale vs loan treatment and state usury, champerty, HIPAA business-associate terms.
ideas.first_90_days: Collect award ledgers (payer, entity, dates) from three groups; fit the payer-behavior model; line up a $25M warehouse; pilot on one Lockstep deal.

ideas.title: Cold Open: neutral price opinion and settlement inside open negotiation
ideas.one_liner: A confidential, non-binding price opinion plus sealed-bid settlement inside the 30-business-day open-negotiation window, so a payer or sponsor can pay a number 'a neutral said' and a provider gets certainty before either spends the dispute toll.
ideas.customer: TPAs, regional payers and sponsors on one side; independent groups and billing firms on the other; both pay per case. First 10: mid-size TPAs and regional Blues, plus sponsor-instructed streams from Sponsor Desk.
ideas.payer_and_signer: TPA VP claims operations or sponsor benefits director; provider revenue-cycle director. Budget: IDR operations cost (~$857 internal per dispute; $2,500 billed back by Premera).
ideas.problem: Open negotiation is a formality (notices by secure email or fax at some plans). The Ops Rule moves it into the portal with a response due by business day 15 and preferred-entity naming, but there is still no neutral voice. Any settlement above QPA looks like a concession, so both sides pay the toll: entity fee $425-$800 to the loser, internal cost, ~54 days average to determination (2024).
ideas.solution: Plumb Line's price opinion plus entity-level outcome data produce a range; each side submits a confidential reservation range; the platform clears inside the overlap; payment through Float; non-precedential by design; the sponsor gets a fiduciary file. Fee ~$100-150 per evaluation plus 1-1.5% of settled value (A).
ideas.why_now: The portal makes the window a structured step for the first time; $15 filings will swamp internal teams; TMA III makes every QPA contestable, so every party wants a neutral view.
ideas.wedge: Low-dollar, high-count categories (pathology/lab, radiology reads, anesthesia) where the toll exceeds the stakes, then ED.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) 2026E ~3.5M disputes (H1 2026 was 1.75M, CMS count). 15% take-up = 525k evaluations x $150 = $79M, plus 40% settling at ~$5k x 1.5% = $16M, about $95M. Needs ~15% of all disputes; heroic unless sponsor instructions from Sponsor Desk supply the volume.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Open-negotiation modules in Zelis NSA Claim Advantage, Claritev and Daffodil (all payer-paid); ADR bodies (AAA, JAMS) with no healthcare payment product at scale that I found; (U) blind-bid claim settlement in auto insurance in the 2000s.
ideas.why_they_lose: IDR entities must stay neutral and cannot predict or advise; carriers cannot name an above-QPA number without precedent; HaloMD is paid on the award; payer-paid vendors are not neutral.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (credibility as a neutral with courts, entities and the Departments) plus network economies once both sides use it.
ideas.earned_secret: Every dispute passes through open negotiation and it is the cheapest point to settle, but no party can be first to name a number; a neutral provides cover. Legal premise to check: confirm settled amounts are not evidence under the contract-history factor; must never be affiliated with an IDR entity (Gavel).
ideas.first_90_days: Settle 200 low-dollar disputes for two TPAs at an opinion price; track settlement rate, days saved and entity fees avoided; get ERISA counsel's view on non-precedent language.

ideas.title: Guild: group-owned IDR and contracting mutual for independent groups
ideas.one_liner: A mutual owned by the independent hospital-based groups, with flat fees, an eligibility warranty and a built-in route into master agreements, aimed at the third of filings that are not from the ten big filers. Weak; flagged.
ideas.customer: Independent anesthesia, radiology, EM, pathology and neonatology groups (U: over a thousand). First 10: ten groups now using a contingency vendor and carrying unpaid awards.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Group managing partner/CFO from the revenue-cycle vendor line (today a share of the award). Members hold equity; patronage dividends return profit.
ideas.problem: Intermediaries win by filing, not collecting. (S) 42% of disputes in late 2025 were challenged as ineligible; (U) Elevance's Georgia suit (May 27 2026) alleges ~70% of HaloMD disputes with a payment were clearly ineligible; the Ops Rule adds 5-business-day information requests with default awards; Pallone's bill sets a 2028 sunset. Independent groups bear the lost fees, the delay and the reputational risk, and no vendor advises converting to contracts.
ideas.solution: Group-owned entity doing flat-fee IDR operations with an eligibility warranty (the mutual eats fees on ineligible closures), pooled outcome data (never prospective prices, for antitrust), a standing conversion pipeline into Lockstep rate cards, and access to Float.
ideas.why_now: Insurer suits against the leading intermediary; the Ops Rule's default regime; a legislative sunset date that makes durable contracts valuable.
ideas.wedge: Eligibility warranty on batched anesthesia and radiology disputes.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Independent groups' share of filings, 31-34%, applied to $15B is $4.7-5.1B in 2025 and $6-7.6B in 2026E. An 8% fee gives a $480-610M pool; $100M is ~20% of it. Heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: HaloMD (27% of resolved disputes in 2025), Pivotal Health, CollectionPro (claims a 92% success rate, U), Zotec and R1 for billing, Waystar; physician societies lobby (ASA, ACEP, ACR) but run no service. No mutual found.
ideas.why_they_lose: A contingency vendor's economics rest on filing volume and a share of the award; an eligibility warranty or a contract recommendation cuts its revenue. A mutual returns profit to members.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning plus member lock-in; pooled data.
ideas.earned_secret: (ED/radiology revenue-cycle director) A group's real yield is cash after ineligible closures, delay and nonpayment, not the headline award; the vendor's yield is filings. Legal premise to check: antitrust on competitor data pooling; reputational risk of helping providers win more; the Pallone sunset.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit 10 founding groups through a state anesthesia or radiology society; audit their last 24 months of closures and unpaid awards; counsel on the mutual structure and clean-team data pooling.

ideas.title: Plumb Line: QPA-of-record after TMA III
ideas.one_liner: The neutral, court-grade verifier of QPAs and benchmark of record: recompute and audit QPAs, issue a per-dispute evidence packet, and give plan fiduciaries a reasonableness opinion for direct contracts.
ideas.customer: Four buyers: providers/billing firms and payers (evidence packets); TPAs and payers (QPA recompute and attestation); plan fiduciaries (opinions on direct contracts); IDR entities and the Departments (reference license). First 10: three independent TPAs facing a recompute, three billing firms, two entities, two sponsors from Sponsor Desk.
ideas.payer_and_signer: TPA chief compliance officer (recompute); provider revenue-cycle director (packets at ~$50 a dispute, A); fiduciary committee (opinions at $2-10k per contract, A); entity COO (license).
ideas.problem: TMA III (Aug 11 2026) struck the federal QPA rules on ghost rates and on excluding bonus/risk-share payments; the replacement rule is pending; whether corrected QPAs reach past claims is open. (U) An industry-funded analysis found reported QPAs below the median in-network rate in ~65% of disputes. Payers cannot pool contracted rates (antitrust) and are conflicted; FAIR Health is an insurer-seeded nonprofit working from allowed amounts; no one is trusted to check.
ideas.solution: Transparent method built from public in-network files (Serif ingests 200+ payers monthly; the Oct 2026 TiC rule moves to network-level, quarterly, attested files) plus payers' attested inputs under NDA plus the IDR public file. Sell (i) QPA recompute for TPAs, (ii) a dispute-level validity and benchmark packet, (iii) fiduciary opinions, (iv) the index that Lockstep rate cards and Cold Open opinions use. Seek recognition by entities and the Departments.
ideas.why_now: Every provider offer will now argue the QPA is invalid and every payer must defend it; the Oct 5 TiC rule raises data quality; Pallone's bill, if enacted, makes a CPI-indexed median contracted rate the price with annual audits, so the method becomes the whole market.
ideas.wedge: Evidence packets for high-count, low-dollar categories (pathology/lab, radiology) and QPA recompute for independent TPAs.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Packets: 3.5M disputes x 25% x $50 = $44M. Recompute/attestation: ~900 payers and TPAs (U) x $75k x 30% = $20M. Opinions: 6,000 plan contracts x $4k = $24M. Entity/regulator licenses plus index licensing $17M. Total ~$105M at 25-30% attach. Heroic but regime-robust.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FAIR Health (NSA Reference File licensed to plans, providers and arbitrators; ~$37M revenue per aggregators, U); PayerPrice (rates and IDR analytics, provider customers only); Turquoise Health and Serif Health (MRF data); Zelis and Claritev QPA services; Daffodil; actuarial consultancies.
ideas.why_they_lose: FAIR Health's governance and data type; PayerPrice is not neutral; payers are conflicted and cannot pool contracted rates; consultancies bill by the hour.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a method accepted by entities, courts and the Departments) plus switching costs when embedded in contract indexes.
ideas.earned_secret: QPA correctness is the load-bearing wall under arbitration (the anchor), reform (the benchmark itself) and direct contracts (the index); whoever the entities trust wins in all three. Legal premise to check: no recompute deadline found (compliance-whiplash risk); antitrust on cross-payer inputs (use public files plus firewalled attestations); never an IDR-entity affiliate.
ideas.first_90_days: Ingest MRFs for the six largest states; reproduce QPAs for ten codes at 20 payers; blind-test against FAIR Health and three payers' disclosed QPAs; meet two entities; pilot with two sponsors.

ideas.title: Gavel: an AI-native, ownership-clean certified IDR entity
ideas.one_liner: Be the 18th certified IDR entity and the first built for the post-June-2026 regime: five-business-day eligibility, 50-line batches, 3.5M-dispute years and a cap table with no provider or payer money.
ideas.customer: The parties, who pay the statutory fee (loser pays, winner refunded; payers lose ~85% of the time). Selection comes from the preferred-entity naming now required of payers in the open-negotiation response, mutual agreement within three business days, or random assignment. First 10: ten TPAs and regional payers that name us for speed, consistency and conflict-clean ownership.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The plan's claims VP who names the entity; the provider revenue-cycle director who can veto it. Price set within CMS's range ($425-$800 single, $625-$1,150 batched for 2-25 lines).
ideas.problem: 17 entities, mostly legacy review shops with salaried clinical reviewers (Maximus, Livanta, IPRO, Acentra, MCMC); volume ~100x the original projection; CMS admits eligibility work is often uncompensated; the $15 fee will raise volume; CMS convened entities Oct 1 2026; four were added since June 2025 and one cannot yet accept cases. Trust is the other problem: 48 organizations asked for a conflict probe (May 14 2026), Pallone wrote to six arbiters, entities are paid only on a determination, and provider win rates vary from 19% to 99% by entity.
ideas.solution: Certify (five years, public petition, no affiliation with plans, issuers, providers or facilities). Build structured intake (registry number, 30-day negotiation compliance, remit codes, fee-paid check), AI-assisted eligibility and packet summarization with licensed human decision-makers, consistent written rationales, published method and audit logs, a sworn no-affiliation statement and no provider/payer capital. Price at the low end of the range. Extend the engine to state IDR programs and other statutory independent reviews as a hedge against a 2028 sunset.
ideas.why_now: The Ops Rule left eligibility with entities on a five-day clock; $15 filings; batching to 50 lines; CMS wants capacity and is adding entities; the conflict probe makes a clean entity valuable to both sides' veto lists.
ideas.wedge: Batched anesthesia, radiology and pathology disputes, where the rule-defined structure is repetitive and the toll per line is lowest.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Entity-fee pool: $1.8B of 2025 admin + entity fees (Georgetown $2.7B cumulative minus $0.885B for 2022-24) minus ~$0.6B admin fees (2.6M disputes x 2 x $115) = ~$1.2B; 2026 is $1.2-1.8B because volume rises but 50-line batches cut fee per line. $100M = 6-8% share; 16 accepting entities average 6.25%. Needs a top-five position, which random assignment alone does not guarantee.
ideas.who_does_it_today: The 17 certified entities: C2C Innovative Solutions, Capitol Bridge, Dane Street, EdiPhy, Federal Hearings and Appeals Services, iMPROve Health, IPRO, Acentra, Livanta (Commence), Maximus Federal, MCMC, MET Healthcare Solutions, National Medical Reviews, Network Medical Review, Medlitix, ProPeer Resources, Provider Resources. Maximus has a case study of AI/RPA running CMS IDR workflows. No AI-native entity found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Labor-based cost; fee ranges prevent price signaling; entanglements with provider capital (U, Leonard Green report); pay-on-determination invites the volume-over-impartiality critique; legacy federal contracts slow change.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a scarce five-year certification) plus process power (a calibrated, auditable decision engine).
ideas.earned_secret: (IDR-entity reviewer) Entity profit is throughput times calibration, not price: the fee is capped and loser-pays. Eligibility triage is five business days of unpaid labor a rules engine can do, and parties strike entities using dispersion data, so consistency is the product. Risks: Pallone's bill would end arbitration for 2028 services; certification timing unknown; independence rules mean no shared ownership, data or staff with the other seven ideas.
ideas.first_90_days: Open the certification file with CMS; hire three former IRO medical directors and two coders; build the rules engine on the 2025 public file and 10k synthetic packets; blind-test consistency; clean the cap table; line up five TPAs to name the entity on day one.

verdicts.title: Harvest Pit Crew

competitors_found.name: Deere Harvester Works harvest-run support
competitors_found.what_they_do: Support vans and a semi trailer of harvest-specific parts follow the harvest run (Altus OK to Minot ND, Munday TX to Conrad MT) and park at dealers; free to Deere owners (2021 account)

competitors_found.name: JD Protect 24-Hour Uptime Assurance
competitors_found.what_they_do: 24-hour uptime assurance with a rental machine on new combines when all maintenance is done at the dealer

competitors_found.name: GleanerCare (AGCO)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Free loaner if a covered combine is not repaired within 24 hours of diagnosis

competitors_found.name: RDO Ready+ and Ready To Harvest
competitors_found.what_they_do: Dealer-backed uptime plan, 200-point pre-harvest inspection, on-farm setup, remote monitoring

verdicts.substitutes: Custom crews run their own mechanics and parts trailers and do emergency field repairs themselves (crew job postings list in-field repairs as operator duties). OEM and dealer harvest support is free or bundled. Fleet-maintenance software is cheap.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 6,000 x $16.5k = $99M is correct arithmetic, but the idea's own custom-crew pool is about 4,000 combines, and USCHI has only about 500 members (crews peaked near 3,000 in the late 1960s). The rest has to come from farms that have dealers and shops. The $12-18k fee is about a crew combine's whole annual repair bill for a response-time promise. Combine sales fell 35.6% to 3,579 in 2025. Realistic ceiling about $12M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Premise 'no brand-agnostic route service' is half true but the OEM/dealer route support exists. A 24-hour-or-credit promise is a service contract, regulated by 43 states and usually needing a reimbursement policy. Deere's settlement is pending court approval, not final.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Deere and dealers already run free harvest-run vans and parts trailers; crews self-repair; the buyer pool is a few hundred crews; the fee approaches the crew's whole repair bill. Too small and partly done.

verdicts.title: Shared Shop

competitors_found.name: Dealer on-site technician and periodic maintenance contracts
competitors_found.what_they_do: Dealers (for example Stewart & Stevenson) offer periodic maintenance contracts and on-site trusted technicians

competitors_found.name: In-house farm shops
competitors_found.what_they_do: Large farms hire their own mechanics (H-2A postings for farm equipment mechanics and service technicians)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Status quo at essentially every large farm

competitors_found.name: Deere JD Protect / PRO Service
competitors_found.what_they_do: OEM maintenance plans and owner-run diagnostics for new Deere machines

verdicts.substitutes: In-house shops with 1-3 techs (cost below $140/hr dealer rates); dealer on-site contracts; independent mobile mechanics.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 500 x $200k = $100M, but most of it is pass-through parts and payroll at cost; at the idea's 15-20% margin that is $15-20M gross profit at full scale. USDA's briefing chart shows about 16k farms at $5M+ across all commodities (including livestock, poultry and nursery), below the idea's 20-25k. Illinois repairs run about $37/acre, so a 6,500-acre farm spends about $240k, consistent with the idea. Realistic: 100-150 accounts, about $25M billings.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: No legal blocker. Premise that nobody sells the outsourced shop is unproven: the only precedent found is a UK 10,000-acre farm, and I found no US demand evidence.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Revenue is mostly pass-through cost, the buyer must give up its own techs, and dealers already sell on-site contracts. Gross profit at the idea's own ceiling is $15-20M.

verdicts.title: Machine Passport

competitors_found.name: Tractor Zoom Pro
competitors_found.what_they_do: Equipment valuations and market data for ag lenders, Farm Credit and dealers; claims 2,250+ auction and dealer locations
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: About $26-27M raised (CB Insights/Dealroom); third-party revenue estimate near $2M (unverified)

competitors_found.name: Machinery Scope
competitors_found.what_they_do: Independent inspections, appraisals and CNA-backed extended warranties on used farm equipment since 2013

competitors_found.name: IronAppraiser (Iron Solutions)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Equipment appraisals used by banks, manufacturers and dealers

competitors_found.name: RB Global / Ritchie Bros inspections
competitors_found.what_they_do: Inspection reports on auction equipment, 600k+ inspections in 2020 across all equipment

verdicts.substitutes: Dealer trade-in appraisals, auction condition reports, free Machinery Pete/TractorHouse listing data, lender in-house collateral reviews.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $27.5M assumes 25,000 inspections at $1,100 against a market price of $100-300 for Machinery Scope inspections (2014 article). $30M assumes 400,000 loans monitored at $75 per year with no buyer evidence. $95-100M needs a quarter of high-value used transactions and a third of lenders, which the idea itself calls heroic. The closest funded peer is estimated near $2M of revenue.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Premise 'no TractorFax, lenders mark collateral blind' is wrong: lenders already buy valuations from Tractor Zoom Pro and IronAppraiser. Data access under the settlement is pending court approval and per-machine owner permission; which fields the tools expose is unverified.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Lender valuation and inspections already exist, prices are 4-10x the market, and the best-funded peer is tiny. Useful as a feeder dataset for a warranty product, not a $100M business alone.

verdicts.title: Tech Bench

competitors_found.name: Trackside Solutions traveling field support technician posting
competitors_found.what_they_do: Traveling field-support techs for OEMs on 2-4 week assignments at $26-30/hr plus per diem

competitors_found.name: Red Seal Recruiting
competitors_found.what_they_do: Places field service mechanics and managers with ag equipment dealers

competitors_found.name: Labor Finders agricultural staffing
competitors_found.what_they_do: Supplies ag equipment technicians, temp-to-hire

competitors_found.name: Dealer road-tech programs
competitors_found.what_they_do: Dealers employ their own road technicians with service trucks

verdicts.substitutes: Dealer recruiting and OEM tech programs, community-college pipelines, generalist diesel staffing firms, flat-rate overtime at the dealer.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 650 x 1,700 x $90 = $99M is correct arithmetic, but the $90 bill rate is wrong. Posted traveling field techs earn $26-30/hr (BLS mean about $52k), so a 25% margin at $90 would imply $65-70/hr pay, about 2.5x market. At a realistic $50-60 bill rate the same 650 FTE is $55-66M, and 650 FTE is not credible in 5-7 years. Workforce Pell (about $1.3-4.3k per trainee) is not revenue.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Workforce Pell began 2026-07-01 but requires a program to have run a year, 150-599 clock hours over 8-14 weeks, 70% completion and 70% placement, and governor and ED approval, so it is not a near-term lever. Travel-nurse analog shows the cycle risk (AMN and Cross Country travel revenue down 37-41%).
verdicts.deciding_reason: Priced 2.5x above market wages, no moat by the idea's own admission, a staffing margin, and existing ag recruiters. Even a good outcome is a $30M staffing business.

verdicts.title: Any-Shop Plan

competitors_found.name: Machinery Scope / Ag Guard (CNA-backed)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Extended service contracts on tractors and combines up to 15 years old, plus inspections and appraisals

competitors_found.name: AmTrust Warranty and Specialty Risk
competitors_found.what_they_do: Extended warranty programs for construction and ag equipment via OEMs and program administrators

competitors_found.name: Assurant with CNH Capital and with EPG
competitors_found.what_they_do: Equipment protection products at point of sale for CNH, and heavy equipment cover for farming, forestry and construction via EPG

competitors_found.name: HSB farm equipment breakdown cover
competitors_found.what_they_do: Breakdown insurance for mobile implements and precision electronics

competitors_found.name: Deere PowerGard and RDO Ready+
competitors_found.what_they_do: Dealer-locked protection plans; PowerGard comprehensive on a new S780 combine quoted $3,500-5,420/yr, limited $550-1,100/yr

verdicts.substitutes: Self-insuring repairs from a farm repair reserve, running a farm shop, OEM plans through the dealer, equipment breakdown insurance, simply buying newer machines.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 20,000 x $5k = $100M uses a combine-level price. Tractors price far lower; at a blended $2k, $100M of premium needs about 50,000 contracts, about 11% of the idea's own unsourced 450k-machine base. As an MGA keeping 25%, revenue is about $25M. Attach rates on ag equipment are described as 'pretty low'. Adverse selection on high-hour used machines is a loss-ratio risk. Realistic revenue about $40M (premium $100M+ only at heroic attach).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Service contracts are regulated by state insurance departments in 43 states (NCOIL), generally on the NAIC Service Contracts Model Act, usually requiring a reimbursement insurance policy or financial-responsibility showing. Solvable but needs a fronting carrier and state-by-state work. The idea's 'NCOIL treats it as insurance' is imprecise.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Structurally the most scalable (balance sheet, lender distribution) but crowded, priced at combine rather than blended levels, and the math lands near $25-40M revenue unless attach reaches about 11% of the base.

verdicts.title: Standard Shop

competitors_found.name: PartsASAP (formerly All States Ag Parts)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Used, rebuilt and aftermarket parts for all makes of ag, construction and industrial equipment; largest buyer of salvage ag equipment
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Kinderhook PE roll-up, 14+ add-ons, 42 locations in 2022; revenue undisclosed

competitors_found.name: Dealer parts counters selling to independents
competitors_found.what_they_do: Average dealer sells parts and tools to 9 independent shops; 56% of dealer parts sold are not installed by the dealer (NAEDA)

competitors_found.name: Deere second-tier parts and price cuts
competitors_found.what_they_do: Cut prices on about 190,000 parts and launching a lower-priced alternative tier through dealers and other retailers; 'Essentials by John Deere' exists

competitors_found.name: AFBF right-to-repair MOUs
competitors_found.what_they_do: Deere, CNH, AGCO, Kubota and CLAAS give farmers and independents manuals, tools and parts help

verdicts.substitutes: Buying parts through the dealer (already common), mail-order suppliers, salvage yards, shops' own supplier relationships.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 500 shops x $200k = $100M needs each shop to run roughly half its parts spend through the program; no census of independent shops exists and the 8-12k figure is the idea's own estimate. Dues of $3.6M are noise. It is a 22-28% margin parts-distribution business competing against Deere's own price cuts. Realistic 100-150 shops, about $25M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: A multi-brand warranty backed by a reinsurer is a service contract and needs the same state licensing. Settlement parity is pending court approval. No legal blocker otherwise.
verdicts.deciding_reason: A parts-distribution margin business at heroic wallet share, squeezed by Deere's price cuts and second-tier parts, with a PE-backed multi-state supplier already serving independents.

verdicts.title: Core Bank

competitors_found.name: John Deere Reman
competitors_found.what_they_do: OEM remanufacturing of 2,000+ products at five Springfield-area sites; core center expanding to 400k sq ft in 2026; sold through dealers

competitors_found.name: CNH Reman via SRC Holdings
competitors_found.what_they_do: CNH reman operation run with Springfield ReManufacturing Corp. since 2009

competitors_found.name: PartsASAP (All States Ag Parts)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Largest buyer of salvage ag equipment with rebuild facilities; used, rebuilt and aftermarket parts
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Kinderhook-backed, 42 locations after the 2022 Romac deal

competitors_found.name: Abilene Machine
competitors_found.what_they_do: Reman combine final drives and hydraulic pumps since 1980, 1-year warranty

competitors_found.name: Texas Final Drive
competitors_found.what_they_do: Reman hydraulic motors and final drives, claims about 50% below new

competitors_found.name: Capital Reman Exchange
competitors_found.what_they_do: OEM diesel engine core sourcing and exchange

verdicts.substitutes: OEM reman through the dealer (the channel independents already use), salvage yards and used parts, new aftermarket parts, rebuilding in the farm's or shop's own bench.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 35,000 exchanges x about $2,900 = about $105M by arithmetic. The event math does not hold: the idea says a 3-5% event rate across about 1M machines makes the pool 'far above 35,000', but 1M x 3-5% = 30-50k events a year, so the plan needs 70-115% of all events; even with several reman-able components per machine it is well over 10%. Realistic 12-18k exchanges, about $40-50M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Settlement terms on reprogramming and parts pairing help electronic-module reman, but access is per machine with owner permission and the order is pending court approval. EPA's Feb 2026 guidance requires equipment to be returned to certified configuration. The 'cores are scarce' claim traces to a core seller's marketing page.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Best structure in the set (core stream as moat), but the event math contradicts itself, OEM reman and a PE-backed 42-location rebuilder already hold the core stream, and independent rebuilders compete on price.

verdicts.title: Elevator Depots

competitors_found.name: John Deere Parts OnSite cabinets
competitors_found.what_they_do: Dealer-managed parts cabinets on the farm, restocked through the dealer, with Deere Financial 'Stock Now. Pay Later' terms

competitors_found.name: Dealer parts counters with delivery
competitors_found.what_they_do: Dealers stock parts, deliver, and call aftermarket the bright spot in 2026

competitors_found.name: Deere second-tier parts via other retailers
competitors_found.what_they_do: Deere will sell its alternative tier at dealers and 'other places customers buy ag parts today', so retailers can buy direct

competitors_found.name: PartsASAP, A&I, Messick's, Sparex
competitors_found.what_they_do: Aftermarket and used parts suppliers to farms, shops and dealers
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: PartsASAP PE-backed with 42 locations; others private

verdicts.substitutes: Dealer counters, Parts OnSite cabinets, mail order, farm stores, farm shops' own parts stock.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 600 depots x $170k = $102M is gross consigned sales. After a 10-12% retailer commission the idea's own contribution is 10-15%, so a $100M-GMV program is a $10-15M business. A rural counter doing $300k-$1M with a $170k incremental depot is also an unproven attach. Realistic: 100-150 depots, about $20M GMV and $3-5M net.

result.pool_note: Pool is real (roughly $12-18B equipment repair; $24.0B includes supplies) and the Deere settlement is real but pending court approval. OEMs and dealers absorb each opening: PRO Service for shops, harvest-run vans, Parts OnSite, price cuts, second-tier parts. Eight thin slices; none reaches $100M revenue without heroic share. Best structure: lender-embedded service contracts.

verdicts.title: The Tele-Inspection Factory

competitors_found.name: Inspected
competitors_found.what_they_do: Tech-enabled Florida private provider doing remote video inspections and alternative plan review for contractors (Permit Hub platform, registered in all Broward cities); also licenses software to code officials via ICC CDS
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Says it has done 100,000+ Florida inspections since 1 Jan 2024 (about 60k a year); $2.2M Series A (https://constructionreviewonline.com/inspected-com-announces-closing-of-2-2m-series-a-financing/), CB Insights shows about $3.25M total; self-described fastest-growing company under $10M revenue; 51-200 employees

competitors_found.name: Inspektr
competitors_found.what_they_do: Guided-video virtual inspection for Florida trade contractors, reviewed same day by a Florida private-provider inspector
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Listed at $99 per inspection per a third-party dossier; funding, volume and Tew & Taylor link unverified

competitors_found.name: Freedom Code Compliance
competitors_found.what_they_do: Licensed Florida private provider under s. 553.791 with multi-county registrations

competitors_found.name: Municipal virtual inspection programs (Tampa/VuSpex, Broward BORA, Miami)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Free city-run live-video or photo inspections for low-risk permits under Florida's 2021 HB 667

verdicts.substitutes: The city's own free virtual inspection programs; in-person private providers who already offer same-day service; contractors simply waiting on the city.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 1.7M inspections a year at $60 is about 28x Inspected's run rate (100k in 20 months, roughly $4-6M a year at $60-99). The idea's own reachable base is 1-1.5M permitted trade finals across all private-provider and fallback states, and Florida is the only state with a virtual-inspection statute, so even 100% of Florida single-trade virtual finals is roughly $60-100M. Price may compress from the idea's $45-75 against a listed $99. The idea's 100k-inspection moat threshold is where the leader already sits with under $10M revenue.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Statute premise is correct: enrolled HB 803 s. 553.791(9) says private-provider inspections may be performed in person or virtually (https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/803/BillText/er/PDF). But the 'no licensed private provider combining software was found' premise is false: Inspected is exactly that. Virtual is barred for structural inspections of threshold buildings; a duly authorized representative must be an employee of the provider.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Already built: Inspected has 100k+ Florida virtual inspections, a Series A, and Broward access since Aug 2025, with under $10M revenue. Low statutory barrier means no moat, and 1.7M inspections is about 28x the leader.

verdicts.title: Inspection-as-a-Service for the Top Homebuilders

competitors_found.name: Universal Engineering Sciences (UES)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Florida engineering firm supplying private-provider plan review and building inspections plus staffing for building departments
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Reported 3,800-4,000+ staff, 80+ branches (older profile said $60M revenue); private

competitors_found.name: Bureau Veritas / CAP Government
competitors_found.what_they_do: Florida building-department outsourcing and private-provider services
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 250+ professionals in CAP at 2022 acquisition; part of Bureau Veritas

competitors_found.name: Florida private providers (share evidence)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Builder-paid private providers already perform a large share of new-home inspections (about 30 per home)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 25% of Pasco inspections FY21, 30% FY22 (about 198,000 inspections); about 35% of passed Jacksonville inspections in one month

competitors_found.name: 2-10 Home Buyers Warranty (Frontdoor)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Insurance-backed structural warranty and builder risk management for new homes
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $585M acquisition; about 1 in 5 new homes (company claim)

competitors_found.name: SiteAware
competitors_found.what_they_do: Digital verification of installed exterior elements for construction QC
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $15M Series B Jan 2022; commercial developers and GCs, not homebuilders

verdicts.substitutes: The private provider the builder already hires; the city inspector; builders' in-house QA teams and forensic QA consultants; third-party quality certifiers such as ACI Inspections.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 80,000 homes is 8.8% of 909,280 US single-family permits in 2025 and roughly a third of FL+GA+TN+UT permits (my estimate; those state counts not retrieved; Texas at 140,002 is fallback-only after a missed city deadline). That is over the 20% heroic line. The defect-data layer is worth only about $235-360 per home (10% of the $2,348-3,602 per-home warranty figures the idea quotes, unverified), well below the $900-1,500 price, so the price rests on city fee substitution, which exists in only a few states and is partly retained by localities as an admin fee ($600 per single-family home in Pasco).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: The s. 553.791(2)(b) rule that localities may not charge plan-review or inspection fees when a private provider does the work is real. But the 25%/50% mandatory fee cut in HB 803 applies only to commercial projects, and localities can still charge a reasonable administrative fee. Texas third-party option depends on HB 14 (missed deadline by 15 days); SB 1450 enactment not confirmed.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Builder-paid private-provider inspections are already 25-35% of inspections in sample Florida counties. Reaching $100M needs about a third of reachable-state homes, and the defect-data premium is a few hundred dollars per home.

verdicts.title: Technical Control plus Latent-Defect Warranty for Attached Housing (an NHBC for the U.S.)

competitors_found.name: 2-10 Home Buyers Warranty (Frontdoor)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Insurance-backed 10-year structural warranties sold to builders; owns the builder relationship
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $585M acquisition; about $198M 2023 revenue per tracker (under $700 per home covered); 1 in 5 new homes (company claim)

competitors_found.what_they_do: Opt-in program trading warranty plus third-party inspection for defect-claim protection; DOLA-run, effective 1 Jan 2026
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: No enrollment data found; condos about 3% of Colorado housing; Pikes Peak issued 64 condo permits in 2025

competitors_found.what_they_do: Existing 10-year structural warranty and mandated building-enclosure inspection; HB 1403 loosens them for ADUs and 12-or-fewer-unit condos

verdicts.substitutes: Builder self-insurance and arbitration (D.R. Horton); existing structural warranty plans; builders simply not building condos; local third-party envelope inspectors.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $100M at $2,800 per home is 36,000 homes a year. The only US analog, 2-10 HBW, earns about $198M across roughly 292k customers (under $700 per home, includes non-structural lines). Colorado produces a few hundred condo units a year at best (Pikes Peak 64 permits in 2025, condos 3% of housing). verdicts.substitutes: Group's own billing staff, existing contingency intermediaries, revenue-cycle vendors, and physician society guidance (ASA, ACEP, ACR) with no service.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Independent groups' 31-34% of filings x $15B = $4.7-5.1B in 2025; 8% fee gives a $480-610M pool; $100M is ~20% of it (idea says heroic). A mutual that returns profit to members cannot fund growth and carries ineligibility-fee risk through its warranty.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Provider-side intermediaries face insurer suits, a 42% ineligibility challenge rate, default closures under the Operations Rule, and the 2028 cutoff in Pallone's bill. Antitrust on competitor data pooling is a further constraint. Idea self-rates 4/10 and flags itself weak.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Crowded, legally exposed provider-side segment with scaled incumbents; mutual structure adds no scale advantage; $100M needs ~20% of the pool.

verdicts.title: Plumb Line: QPA-of-record after TMA III

competitors_found.name: FAIR Health
competitors_found.what_they_do: Nonprofit neutral benchmark; NSA Reference File of median in-network allowed amounts, marketed for IDR use

competitors_found.name: Zelis
competitors_found.what_they_do: QPA analytics inside NSA Claim Advantage; median in-network pricing

competitors_found.name: Turquoise Health
competitors_found.what_they_do: Free open-license out-of-network pricer; sells to insurers; MRF data and QPA/IDR explainer

competitors_found.name: PayerPrice
competitors_found.what_they_do: IDR analytics comparing reported QPA to published negotiated-rate percentiles; provider customers only

competitors_found.name: Serif Health
competitors_found.what_they_do: Payer price transparency analytics and API from MRF data

verdicts.substitutes: Payers computing QPAs in-house, FAIR Health licenses, free Turquoise pricer, provider-side IDR vendors that bundle benchmark evidence, and (if Pallone passes) government audits of 25 plans a year.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Packets: 3.5M x 25% x $50 = $44M, but the three biggest filers (77% of lines) build their own and packets are bundled into IDR software, so the independent-group third gives ~$14M. Recompute: 900 payers/TPAs x $75k x 30% = $20M, but Zelis serves 750+ payers. Opinions $24M and licenses $17M are unsupported. The leading neutral benchmark, FAIR Health, has ~$37M revenue in total, so $105M is almost 3x the incumbent's entire business.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: TMA III (2026-08-11) struck ghost rates and categorical exclusion of bonus/risk-share payments and upheld exclusion of single case agreements, but recompute scope and deadlines and whether corrected QPAs reach past claims are open; no post-ruling agency guidance found. TiC final rule dated 2026-10-05 moves to network-level files; the quarterly and attestation claims came from one vendor blog. Antitrust and non-affiliation with any IDR entity are manageable.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Most regime-robust idea, but the comparable neutral benchmark earns ~$37M, Zelis already ships QPA analytics, and no recompute mandate with a deadline exists yet.

verdicts.title: Gavel: an AI-native, ownership-clean certified IDR entity

competitors_found.name: 17 certified IDR entities (Maximus Federal, IPRO, Acentra, MCMC, C2C, Capitol Bridge, Dane Street, EdiPhy, FHAS, iMPROve, MET, National Medical Reviews, Network Medical Review, medlitix, ProPeer, Provider Resources, Livanta)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Adjudicate federal IDR disputes; fees set within CMS ranges ($200-$840 single, $268-$1,173 batched; Dane Street $595/$695)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: ~$1.3B of entity fees in 2025 across 15 firms

competitors_found.name: Maximus Federal
competitors_found.what_they_do: Largest government-services entity with AI/RPA case study on CMS IDR workflows (per the idea)

competitors_found.name: Zelis, Claritev and Daffodil (adjacent, payer-side AI)
competitors_found.what_they_do: AI on the payer side of IDR; not neutral entities but the only AI-in-IDR products found

verdicts.substitutes: Existing entities that can add automation themselves; the Departments' own IDR Gateway and eligibility screening rules; and the initiating-party selection default.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Pool of ~$1.2-1.3B is real, but share is not winnable by being neutral. The initiating party (nearly always the provider) names the entity and a 3-business-day non-response leaves that choice in place; random selection only applies to disagreement. If ~15% of disputes are randomized, that is ~$225M split 17 ways, ~$13M. The idea's 'random assignment gives 6.25%' and 'payers name us' assumptions both fail. Preferred-entity naming is gated by Gateway rollout (Spring 2027+).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Certification is open on a rolling basis with no stated cap, and 17 entities exist (13 in 2022), so entry is possible. But Georgetown found higher-volume entities ruled more for providers and the lowest-volume entity (about one-third provider wins) handled under 1% of cases; strategic selection by parties is the stated explanation. 'Consistency is the product' is contradicted. Pallone's bill would end IDR for 2028 services.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Providers pick the entity and pick provider-favorable ones; a clean, calibrated entity gets only the randomized remainder (~$13M). Certification is not the barrier; selection is.

result.pool_note: Policy-arbitrage pool: value depends on the QPA/arbitration flaw persisting, yet Pallone's 2028 bill and TMA III threaten it. Zelis (750+ payers) and Claritev (~half of claims) own the payer channel. Providers choose arbitrators, and awards are unenforceable in court in two circuits. The money sits with filers and incumbents, not neutral middlemen.

ideas.title: Zero-Down Copper Exit: pay for the cutover out of the phone bill
ideas.one_liner: Take over the copper exit for multi-site owners at no upfront cost: find every analog life-safety line from the carrier invoices, replace them with one brand-neutral listed communicator per site, and fund it from the POTS charges that stop, with the new recurring contract financed by RMR lenders.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators with 250+ sites: retail and pharmacy chains, bank branch networks, school districts, health systems, self-storage and net-lease REITs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Paid from the telecom opex line (carrier invoices) that the contract shrinks, plus R&M. Signer: Director of Telecom or VP Facilities; CFO countersigns because it is cash-positive from month one.
ideas.problem: Discontinuance notices go to the billing contact, not the person responsible for the fire panel, and a carrier cannot tell whether a line ends at a desk phone, an elevator or a fire panel. These systems do not error out; they lose dial tone and the panel only fails its daily test, which is an impairment (fire watch, insurer notice). Meanwhile the owner pays for two monitored lines per panel at vendor-quoted $150-300 a month (Honeywell dealer flyer; AFA says $60-100 a month saved per building).
ideas.solution: 1) Census: ingest carrier invoices, match each line to a wire center and its public discontinuance date, rank by date. 2) Site pass: tag every analog dependency (fire panel, elevator phone, burglar, door entry, fax/POS) and photograph the panel. 3) Replace with one listed multi-carrier communicator per panel plus analog adapters, and file with the AHJ. 4) 60-month all-in service at about $60-90 a site a month, below the POTS bill, hardware and install carried by us. 5) Finance against the RMR (alarm lenders such as AFS and Rockland Trust already lend on it). 6) Phase 2: the communicator already receives every panel event from any brand, giving cross-OEM telemetry and a verified-ITM score for insurers with no extra hardware.
ideas.why_now: FCC order FCC 26-19 (2026-03-26: 31-day auto-grant, blanket grandfathering); notice periods cut from 180 to 90 days in March 2025; AT&T approved on its first ~500 wire centers and more than 30% of its copper footprint this year with most copper gone by end-2029 outside California (vendor bulletin); Lumen stopped new POTS orders May 2025; POTS rates rising; listed sole-path cellular units exist.
ideas.wedge: A free 'copper census' for 10 operators with 300-3,000 sites (a regional bank, a drugstore or convenience chain, a school district, a health system, a storage REIT). They pay nothing for the audit; we hand them the dated list and the savings.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume $75 a site a month ($900 a year): 110k sites is about $99M a year. Build cost $1,000-1,600 a site (device $300-600; labor, programming, AHJ filing $400-800; census), so $110-175M deployed over about 4 years, financed against RMR (30-40x monthly is $2,250-3,000 of collateral per site; a seller-side broker quotes 45-65x for commercial fire books). Cost to serve about $20-25 a month (wholesale monitoring $5-10, data about $12), gross margin 65-70%, payback 18-21 months. Pool assumption (no source found): 1-2M life-safety copper endpoints, 0.6-1.2M sites in 2026, from 16M switched lines in Dec 2024 falling 17.8% a year (FCC). 110k sites is 9-18% of that pool in 4-5 years: heroic-ish, helped by the top ~150 multi-site operators probably holding 400-500k sites and buying centrally (assumption).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Ooma AirDial (41 reseller partners, 'early days', resellers' POTS cost can exceed what they bill; plus the free POTSTracker lead tool and a Frost & Sullivan leader award), DataRemote POTS-in-a-box, POTSBOX, Telguard (Carrier), Napco StarLink, Resideo/ADI, Honeywell (all boxes); integrators with national accounts (Everon/ADT Commercial, Johnson Controls, Siemens, Convergint, Securitas); telecom expense firms (Tangoe, Calero, Cass) audit invoices and stop at the bill. No owner-side, financed, brand-neutral program found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Box makers sell through dealers and never see the carrier bill. TEM firms do no field work. Integrators bill labor and own the panel relationship, so they will not show a chain that a standard box is the cheapest answer. Honest risk: PE roll-ups pay 45-65x for fire RMR and can subsidize hardware, so they can copy the economics.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (5-year contract, AHJ-registered path); scale economies in carrier and central-station pricing; cornered resource in the per-enterprise line-to-device census plus the wire-center calendar; counter-positioning against dealers once telemetry gives owners independent proof of ITM.
ideas.earned_secret: The only complete inventory of analog lines is the telecom bill, not the facilities register, and carriers retire by wire center, so the order of work is set by a public calendar. The cutover also pays for itself: owners pay for two lines on a panel that can ride a data plan.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the wire-center calendar from AT&T, Verizon and Lumen notices; sign 3 owners for the free census; get wholesale rates from 2 UL central stations; collect alarm-lender term sheets; get 3 AHJs to accept one standard sole-path package; pick the reference listed multi-carrier hardware; check whether public owners can sign multi-year shared-savings telecom contracts.

ideas.title: Wire-Center Sweeps: convert every unconverted small system in a retiring footprint, one visit each
ideas.one_liner: Treat each retiring wire center like a storm-response territory: build the list of every small commercial life-safety system inside it, convert them in one visit with standard kits, and sell the resulting ITM contracts and monitoring to dealers and roll-ups or keep the RMR.
ideas.customer: Owner-managers of restaurants, strip malls, small offices, churches, daycare, clinics and small manufacturers; many have no contractor of record.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Owner or GM from R&M or telecom budgets: $1,200 once plus $45 a month, or zero-down on a 36-month term.
ideas.problem: Same silent dial-tone failure as idea 1, but these owners have no telecom manager, no regional integrator, often no dealer who calls them. Notices go to a billing address. A dead alarm path means a fire watch in many jurisdictions (over 4 hours in Aurora IL, any length in Seattle).
ideas.solution: A calendar of approved wire centers; lists from business registries and public ITM filings; pre-booked crews of 2 techs (one licensed) doing 5-6 swaps a day with pre-programmed communicators; an AHJ packet; a first-year ITM and monitoring contract; an impairment membership (idea 6). Originated contracts are retained or sold.
ideas.why_now: Wire-center-by-wire-center approvals with 90-day notices (one vendor guide says AT&T's first ~500 wire centers were scheduled to begin decommissioning in June 2026; another says forced migrations start the following June, so timing is unclear). Dealers cannot canvass; roll-ups buy books rather than originate.
ideas.wedge: Two approved wire centers in one metro with 800-1,500 businesses each; a 100-door pilot; three AHJs agreeing on the acceptance packet.
ideas.path_to_100m: Price $1,200 install plus $45 a month ($540 a year). Conversions 10k, 25k, 40k in years 1-3; in year 4 at 40k: install $48M plus an RMR base of about 110k sites at $540 is $59M, so about $107M. 40k a year against the assumed 1-2M endpoints leaving copper over about 4 years (250-500k a year) is 8-16% of annual conversions: heroic. It only holds if close rates are about 15% or better and density really lowers cost per swap. Originated ITM contracts may be worth $1,000-2,000 each to a roll-up (assumption; roll-ups pay roughly 1-1.5x revenue for books).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Local alarm dealers on their own base; Pye-Barker and peers buying contract books (22 deals in H1 2026); Ooma POTSTracker plus AirDial resellers (inbound lead gen, not field density); carriers only send notices.
ideas.why_they_lose: Dealers sell to existing customers within a 30-40 mile radius; roll-ups pay about 1x revenue to buy what a sweep originates for a few hundred dollars of CAC; resellers wait for inbound; carriers cannot recommend vendors.
ideas.moat: Route density (scale economies) and the originated-contract book; calendar and list data.
ideas.earned_secret: Deadlines are by wire center, so demand arrives as local waves. A crew that has done 200 swaps in one wire center has a lower cost per swap than any dealer, and a swap is the cheapest moment in the industry to originate an ITM contract.
ideas.first_90_days: Choose 2 wire centers with approved dates; build lists; sign licensed subs in the state; run the 100-door pilot; test price points; sign a wholesale monitoring agreement; line up one roll-up as buyer of originated contracts; confirm door-to-door rules and permit needs.

ideas.title: Second-Opinion Desk: free quote checks that become the owner's neutral fire-and-life-safety program
ideas.one_liner: Check any deficiency quote for free against a price book and competing bids, then become the owner's single contract, bidding and records layer for fire and life safety across all sites, paid from the savings.
ideas.customer: Owners with 50-5,000 sites: REITs, retailers, banks, K-12 and universities, health systems, hotels.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Existing ITM and repair budget. VP Facilities or Director of Risk. Fee 8-12% program fee, or principal margin of 20-25% when we hold the contract.
ideas.problem: ITM is the loss leader; the deficiency list is the product. Cintas Fire Protection runs about a 50% gross margin (49.3% Q4 FY25, 50.8% Q4 FY26) and one platform reports $822M of repair revenue tied to recurring inspections across its customers in 2025. The owner cannot judge whether a deficiency is urgent or fairly priced. Programming files and passwords sit with the contractor although NFPA 72 lists the site-specific software and passwords among the items the installer delivers. Public owners keep signing sole-source awards to the incumbent.
ideas.solution: 1) Free quote check: upload a quote, get a price comparison and an urgency call by a former sprinkler contractor. 2) A price database built from partner price books and bids. 3) Bid rounds across vetted local contractors. 4) Program mode: one contract, one set of reports, AHJ filings and one invoice, with a quarterly benchmark. 5) A records vault (as-builts, site-specific software, passwords, ITM history) so any contractor can take over.
ideas.why_now: Roll-up price increases (anecdotal), labor shortage, owner budget scrutiny, and the copper cutover pushing capital questions onto fire budgets.
ideas.wedge: Free quote checks for 20 mid-size owners (K-12 districts, bank networks), 5 converted to program mode.
ideas.path_to_100m: Principal revenue. Assume $2.5-4k a year per site of ITM plus repairs, so $100M is 25-40k sites. Assume 1.5M+ sites sit with owners that have 50+ sites (assumption), so 2-3% of sites: not heroic on share. But at 20-25% gross margin that is $20-25M of gross profit; the real value is the price database, the vault and the contractor network.
ideas.who_does_it_today: National-account arms of JCI, Everon, Siemens, Convergint, Securitas, Cintas and Pye-Barker; facilities outsourcers (JLL, CBRE, Cushman); marketplaces (ServiceChannel, Corrigo, SMS Assist); contractor tools (ServiceTrade with 1,300+ contractors, Inspect Point, Ember). No neutral, fire-specific, owner-side second opinion found (not exhaustive).
ideas.why_they_lose: Contractors earn their margin on repairs. Outsourcers earn pass-through margin on subs. Marketplaces lack fire-code competence to say a deficiency is not urgent. None can credibly promise neutrality.
ideas.moat: Network economies (price data improves with every quote); switching costs (the vault); counter-positioning against repair-margin contractors.
ideas.earned_secret: A repair quote is priced by who holds the panel passwords, not by what the work costs.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 3 friendly contractors for price books; run the quote checker free for 20 owners; get read access to AHJ reports through owners' Compliance Engine accounts; hire a former fire marshal for urgency calls; run the first bid round.

ideas.title: Panel Liberation: zero-down replacement of locked proprietary fire panels
ideas.one_liner: Move owners off panels that only one dealer can program onto open-protocol panels with zero-down monthly pricing, hand over the programming files and passwords, and bid out the ITM, paid from the lock-in premium the owner stops paying.
ideas.customer: Owners with legacy Simplex, Edwards or Siemens estates, especially public bodies that keep writing sole-source justifications: universities, school districts, municipalities, hospitals.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Capital or R&M budget; Director of Facilities with purchasing. Zero-down is paid from the service premium the owner stops paying.
ideas.problem: A NIST sole-source notice says Simplex's proprietary protocols mean only the Simplex dealer can modify and reprogram; a Palm Beach County agreement says the programming software is available only to factory-trained technicians; Worcester's DCU Center cites end-of-life panels and Simplex compatibility for a sole-source. Forum technicians say addressable devices rarely cross brands. The owner pays a premium and cannot get competitive bids.
ideas.solution: Audit which panels are locked or end-of-life; replace with open-protocol panels any certified dealer may program (check each brand's dealer rules); reuse wiring and conventional devices where possible; hand over site-specific software and passwords at close-out; install the standard communicator (idea 1) in the same visit; bid the ITM; finance on a monthly fee below the current service premium.
ideas.why_now: The copper cutover forces a visit to every panel anyway; older panels are going end-of-life (Alameda County replaced a Siemens MXL with end-of-service in 2018; Worcester; a Treasury sole-source for three panels at $50-200k); sole-source rules bite public owners.
ideas.wedge: A free 'liberation audit' of 10 universities and school districts with Simplex 4100 estates.
ideas.path_to_100m: Bid data: $50-200k for three panels, $600-625k for three buildings (Cornell), vendor guides $5k to $25k+ per installed panel. Assume $20k average: 5,000 replacements a year is $100M. Assume 60-80k panel replacements a year nationally (assumption, no source), so 6-8% of annual flow.
