After three years about 15k liberated sites at $3-4k a year of ITM, monitoring and repair adds $45-60M recurring. Heroic-ish; the installed base of locked panels is unverified.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Every fire contractor does panel replacements; OEM dealers (JCI/Simplex, Honeywell, Siemens, Carrier/Edwards) and national integrators. No one found selling 'escape from lock-in' as the product.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEM dealers' service annuity depends on the lock; they cannot advertise 'leave us'. Independent contractors lack capital and a standard migration process.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against OEM dealers; process power in a repeatable migration; fleet data on which panels are locked and when they fail.
ideas.earned_secret: The lock is passwords and protocol, not safety. Most field wiring and many devices can be reused, and the AHJ only needs re-acceptance testing.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick 5 public owners; run the audit; pre-clear two open panel families against their manufacturers' dealer rules; agree acceptance testing with 3 AHJs; line up a financing partner. Risks to test: a specialist argues upgrading the panel is cheaper than replacing the system, some OEMs restrict reuse.

ideas.title: Full-Service Fire Protection: one flat price per square foot a year, repairs included
ideas.one_liner: Sell mid-size owners ITM, monitoring and all routine repairs for one flat annual price per square foot, priced from fleet data and backed by contractual liability insurance, which time-and-materials contractors cannot offer without destroying their repair margin.
ideas.customer: Owners with 5-100 buildings: school districts, small REITs, hospital groups, hotel owners, universities.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The ITM and repair budget; Director of Facilities or CFO who wants budget certainty. Assumed price $0.20-0.40 per square foot a year.
ideas.problem: Surprise deficiency bills several times the ITM price, slow capital approvals, and impairments that linger. Incumbents cannot fix it: repair is their profit engine (about 50% gross margin at Cintas Fire) and OEM dealers earn parts margin. Elevator contracts are routinely sold as full-maintenance agreements, but fire protection is sold inspection-only.
ideas.solution: Price each building from age, panel brand, system types and ITM history; use the idea 1 event stream to cut visits and predict failures; include a 4-hour impairment response (idea 6) and an AHJ-pass guarantee; exclude abuse and new code upgrades; five-year terms; contractual liability or reimbursement insurance where state service-contract law requires it.
ideas.why_now: Roll-up price increases, labor shortage, telemetry arriving through the cutover, and owners wanting predictable opex.
ideas.wedge: 20 school districts and 10 small REITs, starting with fire alarm and extinguishers only, adding sprinklers after the first loss data.
ideas.path_to_100m: Average building 50k sf at $0.30 is $15k a year; 6,700 buildings is $100M. Assume 400-600k buildings sit with owners of 5-100 buildings (assumption), so 1.1-1.7% of buildings: not heroic on share. The risk is the loss ratio: gross margin must hold at 30% or better and adverse selection must be capped by building-age bands. Legal check: service-contract regulation varies by state (registration, reimbursement insurance); round 1 lost ideas to insurance reclassification.
ideas.who_does_it_today: JCI, Siemens and Honeywell managed services and performance contracts for large accounts; Cintas (route-based); contractors' inspection-only agreements. No one found selling flat-fee all-in fire protection broadly (not exhaustive).
ideas.why_they_lose: Their pricing model punishes prevention. A hybrid entrant needs a lower cost to serve through telemetry and route density.
ideas.moat: Underwriting data (process power); switching costs on five-year terms; counter-positioning against T&M repair margins.
ideas.earned_secret: Technician view, unverified: a small set of components (batteries, detectors, flow switches, pump controllers, backflow) drives most repair spend, and their failure timing is predictable from age and trouble logs.
ideas.first_90_days: Get 24 months of ITM and repair history from 5 owners; fit a price model; pilot 200 buildings with a contractor holding the labor; line up a reimbursement insurer; check service-contract law in the first two states.

ideas.title: Impairment Desk: the first four hours after any fire system goes out of service
ideas.one_liner: A 24/7 desk that handles the hours after a fire alarm or sprinkler system is out of service (copper cut, panel fault, valve closed, construction shutoff): mobilize a remote or roving fire watch, notify the AHJ, central station and insurer with a time-stamped record, and dispatch the repair.
ideas.customer: Owners of monitored commercial buildings (membership); general contractors on wood-frame builder's risk; central stations, dealers and roll-ups (white label); hospitals for interim life safety measures.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Owners: operations or risk budget; property manager or Director of Risk. GCs: security and fire-watch general conditions; project executive or risk manager. Insurers indirectly via premium credits.
ideas.problem: Four silos and nobody owns the hours between failure and fix. Guard companies sell hours, not outcomes (remote watch cannibalizes them); contractors repair but do not staff watches or file notices; central stations cannot call owners directly (the dealer is their customer); insurers cannot mandate vendors. NFPA: sprinklers operated in 92% of fires where present and large enough, and when they failed the leading reason was a shut-off system (three-fifths in 2010-14). ISO CP 04 11 protective-safeguards endorsements make keeping the sprinkler system in service a condition of coverage and require notifying the insurer of impairments (IRMI notes a 48-hour exception for certain shutoffs). Many AHJs require a fire watch for impairments over 4 hours (Aurora IL), 8 hours (Syracuse) or any length (Seattle); private fire watch quotes run $35-150 an hour.
ideas.solution: Intake from central-station failure-to-communicate lists and tamper alarms, owner calls and communicator telemetry (idea 1); mobilize a vetted on-call guard network plus camera and thermal analytics where the AHJ or insurer accepts them (FM Approvals Standard 3270 now covers remote fire watch systems, BlackStarTech FireSight certified for hot work); record AHJ, insurer and central-station notices and the restoration log; dispatch a licensed contractor with parts. Price: membership $15-40 a site a month, per-event fees, a monthly per-site price for builder's risk.
ideas.why_now: Copper cutovers create a wave of silent path failures; FM 3270 and insurer openness to technology; wood-frame builder's risk markets have asked for 24-hour guards (2018 broker note); guard wage inflation.
ideas.wedge: Builder's-risk fire watch for wood-frame multifamily (clear existing budget; the insurer, not the AHJ, decides acceptance), then impairment memberships through two central stations.
ideas.path_to_100m: All volumes are assumptions; no fire-watch market number was found. Membership: 100k sites at $360 a year is $36M (about 5% of an assumed 2M monitored commercial fire accounts). Events: 40k events a year at 50 hours and $30 net is $60M (13% of an assumed 300k impairment events a year). Builder's risk: 150 sites at $90k a year is $13.5M. About $110M total, heroic on every leg. It is dead unless AHJ impairment-notification logs show the real event count.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Guard companies' fire-watch services (Allied Universal, Securitas, GardaWorld and local fire-watch guard firms); alarm contractors' emergency service; BlackStarTech FireSight (hot work); central-station call lists; insurers' risk engineers. No one found owning the whole sequence.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each incumbent owns one silo and loses revenue by adopting the missing piece (the guard industry by remote watch, dealers by exposing central-station data, contractors by pricing outcomes).
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against guard hours; AHJ and insurer acceptance as a cornered resource; on-call network density.
ideas.earned_secret: Central-station view: the failure-to-communicate list is the first sign of an impairment. The real cost is the scramble, because most owners learn about the fire-watch requirement and the insurer-notice duty from an operator reading a script.
ideas.first_90_days: File public-records requests for impairment notifications in 5 cities; map which AHJs accept remote watch; get one builder's-risk carrier to accept an FM 3270 system; sign a guard network in two metros; pilot with two central stations.

ideas.title: Hyperscale Life-Safety Crew: the scarce-trade play behind the data-center build
ideas.one_liner: A specialist prime for data-center fire detection, suppression and integrated systems testing, plus ITM for operating halls, with an in-house apprenticeship academy and prefabrication to relieve the scarce-labor constraint.
ideas.customer: Hyperscalers, colocation operators, and the GCs and MEP primes that build for them.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Capex line for fire and life safety; Director of Construction or VP Critical Environments; GC procurement.
ideas.problem: Pattern: capex-supercycle pass-through to scarce physical trades (Comfort Systems, Quanta, IES): enter through the scarce input. My inference for why it is not done as a stand-alone specialist: fire protection is bought as a subtrade inside the MEP package. Census data-center construction ran at $50.7B annualized in April 2026 (+28% year on year; June +46%). A 2026 trade source puts fire suppression at 2.5-4% of construction cost (weak source); a secondary summary says 29% of the fire protection workforce is expected to retire by 2026 with 14-20% shortfalls.
ideas.solution: Design-build packages for aspirating detection, pre-action and clean agent; integrated systems testing on its own schedule and budget; frame agreements that reserve capacity; an apprenticeship academy paid by customers' capacity reservations; prefab riser and header assemblies; ITM contracts for operating halls.
ideas.why_now: AI capex has pushed data-center construction past $50B a year and skilled fire-protection labor is the binding input.
ideas.wedge: Commissioning and integrated testing for two colocation builders in one metro, then installation.
ideas.path_to_100m: $50.7B x 2-3% is $1.0-1.5B a year of fire and life-safety install work; integrated testing adds an assumed $100-250M; operating-hall ITM adds more. $100M is 7-10% of the install and testing pool. Heroic-ish and cyclical.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Johnson Controls, Siemens, Convergint, APi Group, Comfort Systems USA and EMCOR fire protection units; regional sprinkler primes; commissioning agents; engineering firms such as Jensen Hughes.
ideas.why_they_lose: Generalist primes spread scarce techs across all customers and do not offer reserved capacity. This is a focus and labor advantage, not a business-model conflict.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource in trained labor (the academy); process power in testing; long frame agreements.
ideas.earned_secret: From memory, unverified: in a data hall the cost is not the system but the false discharge (a gas release has knocked out disk arrays before). Hyperscalers pay for people who have run the test sequence before.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit a commissioning lead; pick the two builders; secure a training partner; price an integrated-testing package. Risks: capex pullback, hyperscalers self-perform, large primes buy the labor.

ideas.title: Hood-to-Alarm Program for restaurant franchise systems
ideas.one_liner: Sell the 20-30 largest restaurant franchisors and purchasing co-ops one program for hood cleaning (NFPA 96), kitchen suppression, extinguishers and alarm and sprinkler ITM, with proof of service for insurers and AHJs.
ideas.customer: Franchisors, their supply-chain arms and co-ops; franchisees.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Franchisee R&M, mandated by brand standards. Signer: franchisor VP Operations or supply chain; co-op CEO.
ideas.problem: Pattern: concentrated-operator vertical platform (a few dozen operators control many locations and run the same repetitive function). Not done because hood cleaners (thousands of small firms and one franchise brand) and fire contractors are different trades, so no one bundles cleaning, suppression, extinguishers and alarm with a single proof of service. Hoodz (BELFOR Franchise Group) ran a National Account Program and an executive once called kitchen exhaust cleaning one of the few recurring services chains still buy site by site.
ideas.solution: One national program with local subs: scheduled hood cleaning, semiannual suppression service, extinguishers, alarm and sprinkler ITM, a single compliance record that insurers and AHJs can query, sold through franchisor approved-supplier status.
ideas.why_now: Insurers and landlords ask for service certificates; labor shortages in cleaning; franchisors seeking one national vendor for compliance.
ideas.wedge: A 200-unit pilot with one franchisor or co-op in two metros.
ideas.path_to_100m: Hood cleaning runs about $1,200-4,500 a year (price guides); suppression, extinguishers and alarm ITM add about $1-2k. Assume $4k per restaurant: 25k restaurants is $100M as principal. About 731k restaurants with employees and about 70% independent (vendor estimate) implies roughly 220k chain units (assumption), so about 11% of chain units: heroic, but one franchisor decision moves 500-5,000 units.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Hoodz (BELFOR Franchise Group), local cleaners, Cintas (extinguishers and suppression), Pye-Barker, JCI/Ansul dealers, and FM platforms (ServiceChannel, Corrigo, SMS Assist) that route tickets.
ideas.why_they_lose: Hoodz is a cleaning franchise with local variance; fire contractors do not clean; FM platforms do not own compliance proof.
ideas.moat: Franchisor approval as a cornered resource; a compliance record insurers can query.
ideas.earned_secret: Unverified: insurers and landlords care about the cleaning certificate and suppression tag, and a missing record is what hurts after a kitchen fire.
ideas.first_90_days: Meet 5 franchisor operations VPs; pick a 200-unit pilot; sign local cleaners and a suppression contractor in two metros; ask 2 insurers what proof they accept.

ideas.title: Retro-Flag: post-adjudication 340B correction rail for state Medicaid
ideas.one_liner: Take the 340B status that administrators assign days after a script is filled, push it back into the state Medicaid or MCO claim, reprice at acquisition cost, and invoice manufacturer rebates only on units that qualify, paid out of the rebates recaptured.
ideas.customer: State Medicaid agencies (fee-for-service and managed care) and the MCOs/PBMs under them. First: Louisiana (live carve-out and claim-level rules), Indiana (proposed end of Medicaid reimbursement for 340B drugs, FQHCs exempt), Illinois (SB3878 introduced).
ideas.payer_and_signer: State Medicaid pharmacy program (rebate-administration and program-integrity budget), signed by the State Medicaid Director with the pharmacy program manager; MCO side signed by the chief pharmacy officer. Fee about 10% of net incremental rebates and avoided disputes (my estimate), so the state sees cash recapture rather than a new line item.
ideas.problem: The statute bars a duplicate discount (a unit gets a 340B price or a Medicaid rebate, not both). States use a provider-level Medicaid Exclusion File (50% of HRSA's FY25 adverse audit findings involved duplicates/MEF; 5 of 28 MEF findings were administrative only), claim flags that NCPA calls largely unusable under the replenishment model, or blunt bans: Louisiana forbids contract pharmacies from billing Medicaid for 340B-priced drugs and from 1 Jan 2026 seeks rebates claim by claim on physician-administered drugs under CMS-2434-F. Louisiana's six MCOs each run their own PBM since 1 Oct 2025; Aetna's is CVS Caremark, whose parent owns the Wellpartner 340B administrator.
ideas.solution: (1) TPAs, covered entities and pharmacies post retroactive 340B assignments by claim. (2) The service matches each to the payer's claim. (3) It issues NCPDP reversal/rebill or state-specific adjustment files. (4) It marks each claim rebate-eligible or excluded for state and MCO rebate invoicing. (5) It stores the evidence manufacturers demand in disputes. Covered entities get the same record as HRSA-audit proof. Legal premise: the duplicate-discount ban is statutory and Louisiana shows claim-level rules are workable, but hospital groups litigate and states are exempting FQHCs, so sell a claim-level control, not a ban.
ideas.why_now: Louisiana's rules took effect Oct 2025 and Jan 2026; CMS-2434-F makes physician-administered drug rebates mandatory; H.R.1 cuts federal Medicaid by $911B over 2025-34 (KFF, read in the pool file), so states want cash; Manatt surveyed all 50 states in July 2026; 19 states enacted 22 340B bills in 2025.
ideas.wedge: Louisiana fee-for-service (vendor: Gainwell) plus one MCO, or Indiana before its policy starts. First 10: 3 states, 4 MCOs, 3 TPAs as data partners. Offer a recapture-only contract: no fee unless rebates are recaptured.
ideas.path_to_100m: Take PhRMA-funded BRG's estimate that 340B pulled $6.5B of Medicaid rebates in 2024 ($4.2B federal, $2.3B state) as a ceiling, not a fact. If the 15 largest Medicaid-managed-care states (about 70% of spend, my estimate) each recapture 25% of their pro-rata share: 0.7 x $6.5B x 25% = about $1.14B; a 10% fee = about $114M. Needs 15 states, over a third of the market (Medicaid rebates total about $58.4B, KFF FY2024). If the true loss is a third of BRG's number the ceiling is about $40M and the idea is dead unless it extends to Part D MFP and commercial.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Gainwell (Louisiana fee-for-service point-of-sale), MCO PBMs (CVS Caremark, Optum Rx, Express Scripts, Prime), HRSA's Medicaid Exclusion File, Kalderos (sells to manufacturers, so it disputes the state's invoices), state audit contractors, Apexus (free guidance).
ideas.why_they_lose: The MCO's PBM owns the 340B pharmacy and administrator profits it would have to police; Gainwell is paid per transaction and system build, not recapture; Kalderos works for the party being invoiced; nobody holds the TPA-side feed.
ideas.moat: Network economies (every TPA integrated improves every state's data, and each state rule pulls in more TPAs) plus switching costs inside point-of-sale and MMIS integrations.
ideas.earned_secret: In the replenishment (virtual-inventory) model nobody at the counter knows whether a script is a 340B script; the administrator decides days later, after the payer has paid and the state has invoiced the manufacturer. Every 'flag it at the point of sale' policy is a fiction; only a correction loop works. Also, the 340B ceiling price is AMP minus the same unit rebate amount that sets the Medicaid rebate, so the manufacturer pays the same either way and the real fight is states against hospitals. (Insider claim; verify with 10 TPA staff.)
ideas.first_90_days: Reconcile 12 months of Louisiana claims against a TPA's retro assignments as a free sample; sign data MOUs with two TPAs; hire an ex-state rebate analyst; map NCPDP reversal flows with two PBM vendors; get a counsel memo on state authority; pitch Indiana and Illinois staff.

ideas.title: Route Desk: per-unit 340B / MFP / non-340B router for health systems
ideas.one_liner: A decision engine on the hospital's virtual inventory that assigns each administration and fill to 340B, MFP or non-340B, paid a share of the margin it preserves; the first tool for the three policies that cap 340B value at once.
ideas.customer: DSH health systems (79% of 340B dollars: $79.2B of $100B in 2025), then the other 340B hospitals paid under OPPS (CMS counts 1,957 eligible 340B hospitals).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Hospital CFO co-signed with the chief pharmacy officer; pharmacy purchasing and revenue-cycle budgets. Success fee 15-20% of preserved or added margin against a baseline (my estimate).
ideas.problem: If CMS finalizes its July proposal, 340B-acquired separately payable Part B drugs are paid ASP minus 33.4% from 1 Jan 2027 (JG), exempt hospitals use TB, everything else XX at ASP+6%. CMS estimates $4.85B of lower drug spending (others say about $5.7B). Its survey found 340B drugs bought at 33.4% below ASP and non-340B at 2.7% above, so the 340B route earns (discount minus 33.4%) of ASP while the non-340B route earns about +3.3%: break-even discount is about 37%. Roughly half of NDC volume sits below that if discounts vary about 20 points around the mean (my assumption). MFP adds a 'lower of' rule (Walgreens routes all 2026 selected-drug Part D scripts to MFP, not the 340B pilot) and states are carving Medicaid out. Today the choice is made by administrators and software paid on 340B volume.
ideas.solution: An NDC x payer x site x pharmacy table (HRSA ceiling price, WAC, GPO price and ASP, MFP, state Medicaid policy, contract rate) feeds assignments into the accumulator, ties JG/TB/XX claims back to purchase evidence for audit, and trues up monthly. Legal premise: choosing non-340B stock for a unit is lawful because 340B is elective, but DSH, children's and cancer hospitals are barred from GPO purchasing of outpatient drugs (the statute stands; a D.D.C. ruling on 31 Mar 2026 vacated HRSA's 2013 replenishment limits and HRSA can re-adopt them), and CMS's final rate and exemptions may change. The engine is parameterized so a different final rate only moves the break-even.
ideas.why_now: Final OPPS rule due about 1 Nov; the remedy offset rises from 0.5% to 3.0% of the conversion factor for pre-2018 hospitals (about $2.3B in 2027); the rebate pilot starts the same day; the AHA suit is pending; MFP list grows from 10 to 25 drugs in 2027.
ideas.wedge: Medicare Part B for 10 DSH systems with heavy oncology and infusion. Give each a free 'Day-One map' built from public ASP and ceiling data in exchange for a three-year success-fee contract signed before 1 January.
ideas.path_to_100m: Part B 340B payment base is about $13B ($4.85B / 0.37, my derivation), about $12B of ASP value. With NDC discounts spread +/-20 points, routing is worth about 10% of ASP value (about $1.2B gross; about half realizable = $0.6B). Add MFP routing (about $0.4B, my estimate) and Medicaid carve-outs (about $0.2B): about $1.2B preserved x 20% = about $240M at 100% adoption, so $100M needs about 40% of the addressable margin. HEROIC SHARE. The credible route is an enterprise platform for the top ~100 systems at $0.5-1M a year plus the success fee. Hospital-side software is a small pool: Craneware's whole company is $206M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Sentry (Craneware; serves about 40% of hospitals; FY26 revenue $206M flat, FY27 guided to about $185M), Pillr (300+ hospitals; split billing, rebate readiness; Water Street-owned since Jan 2026), Wellpartner and Walgreens 340B Complete (administrators paid on spread), Bluesight (compliance), Apexus (free education), consultancies for one-off modeling, EHR 340B modules (general knowledge).
ideas.why_they_lose: Administrators and software vendors are paid on 340B volume, so telling a hospital to stop claiming a unit cuts their own revenue; consultancies attached to audit firms cannot take contingent fees from audit clients (general rule; verify); EHRs cannot see the wholesaler and pharmacy sides.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (incumbents can't recommend un-340B without cannibalizing) plus data scale: NDC-level realized discounts across hospitals that no single hospital has.
ideas.earned_secret: 340B is a per-unit election, not a status. CMS's own numbers make the Medicare 340B route worth less than the WAC route for about half of NDCs, and nobody on the hospital's payroll is paid to say so. (Insider claim; verify with 10 340B directors.)
ideas.first_90_days: Build the break-even table by NDC from public files the day the final rule drops; run it for 10 systems; sign success-fee contracts; integrate with one administrator's accumulator; get a written HRSA/CMS counsel view on payer-specific accumulation; track the AHA suit.

ideas.title: Cass for 340B: audit-and-pay hub for drug purchases, fees and remittances
ideas.one_liner: Freight audit-and-pay for drugs: an independent hub that audits every 340B invoice, credit-and-rebill, pharmacy fee and remittance against ceiling prices and contracts, pays the clean ones, and advances cash against contract-pharmacy remittances.
ideas.customer: Mid-size and rural covered entities and FQHC networks first; large systems later.
ideas.payer_and_signer: CFO or treasurer (advances) and the director of pharmacy purchasing or VP revenue cycle (audit). Contingency about 25% of recovered dollars plus an advance spread.
ideas.problem: Apexus notes credit-and-rebill options 'have timeframe restrictions based on invoice date'; vendors describe invoice lines stuck at WAC, restored 340B prices that never appear, and late or wrong-quantity credits. Pharmacy and administrator fees are percentage-of-spread (Wellpartner: greater of $4 or 10% of reimbursement minus ceiling, rising to 14% by year three; GAO 2018 found $23 flat, $19 + 16% and $8 + 20% of spread structures). Nobody reconciles price paid to ceiling price across time. Why it hasn't happened here: there is no payer in the middle of the 340B chain; administrators are paid on claims, wholesalers are the counterparty, hospital payables are automated, and chain administrators control remittance timing.
ideas.solution: Stage 1: contingency audit of 12-24 months of invoices (EDI feed only). Stage 2: audit of pharmacy and administrator fees against contract. Stage 3: a lockbox plus advances (about 90% of expected remittance on day 3); obligors are investment-grade chains (CVS, Walgreens, Cigna, UnitedHealth, Walmart), so credit risk is mostly theirs. Cass Information Systems shows the model elsewhere: $190.8M of 2025 revenue ($66.1M processing fees, $40.4M financial fees, $81.2M net interest) on about $94B of annual freight payments, a yield near 0.2%.
ideas.why_now: 340B purchases are growing about 20% a year; hospitals are about to lose Medicare margin and treasuries will be tight; the rebate pilot makes payment timing a live issue for the first time.
ideas.wedge: 10 critical-access hospitals and FQHC networks; audit free for the first 90 days and keep 25% of recoveries.
ideas.path_to_100m: At Cass's 0.2% yield $100M needs about $50B of flows, half of all 340B purchases, so float cannot carry it. Three streams, assumptions flagged: (a) invoice/credit leakage of 0.4% of $100B = $400M, recover 60% = $240M, fee 25% = $60M; (b) pharmacy/administrator fee overbilling of 2% of a ~$4-5B fee pool = about $90M recovered, fee 25% = about $22M; (c) advances of ~$0.7B average balance at 9% = about $63M gross (needs ~$0.7B capital). About $140M at 100% share. HEROIC SHARE (70%+), and it works only if leakage is at least 1% of purchases. Kill criterion: if the first 20 audits find under 0.4%, stop. Adding manufacturer-side chargeback validation raises the ceiling.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Apexus (free price-verification guidance), Bluesight (inventory and invoice reconciliation), Sentry, Pillr, Wellpartner and Walgreens (own reconciliation), wholesaler 340B support desks, manufacturers' chargeback validation (Vistex, Model N; general knowledge).
ideas.why_they_lose: Wholesalers cannot audit themselves; administrators are paid on claims, not price accuracy; chains hold the float; Big-4 firms audit the health systems and cannot take contingent fees from them.
ideas.moat: Process power (an audit rule set refined on every recovery) and switching costs once payables run through the hub.
ideas.earned_secret: The leak is in retroactive reclassification: units are bought at WAC, then credited to 340B after accumulation, inside windows no one owns. The administrator reconciles to claims, the wholesaler to invoices, accounts payable to purchase orders. (Insider claim; the leakage rate is unpublished.)
ideas.first_90_days: Audit invoices for 5 free pilots and measure leakage; get HRSA ceiling-price access as a covered-entity agent; line up a lender for the advance facility; price against Wellpartner's fee schedule.

ideas.title: Switzerland: hospital-governed, manufacturer-funded 340B claims trust
ideas.one_liner: A claims trust owned by hospitals and health centers that holds the unit-level ledger behind a firewall and returns only pass/fail and payment; the rail the Senate bill calls an independent clearinghouse, built before the law and usable under all three political outcomes.
ideas.customer: Manufacturers (platform and duplicate prevention), covered entities (claims submission and rebate operations), states (Medicaid ID), later HRSA or a Senate-designated operator.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Manufacturer VP Government Pricing or chief compliance officer pays per verdict and per rebate processed (HRSA requires manufacturers to bear platform cost); covered entities pay outcome-priced operations (2-3% of rebates collected, my estimate); HRSA or CMS pays under any clearinghouse law.
ideas.problem: Everyone agrees claims-level data stops duplicates; the fight is what it is used for. Hospitals say it will be used to deny rebates and trigger audits; manufacturers say without it they cannot stop duplicates. HHS puts the pilot's burden on covered entities at $537M a year, the AHA over $1B; claims are due in 45 days and a rebate must be paid or formally denied in 10. Why it hasn't happened: both live platforms belong to one side. Kalderos (Truzo; 'thousands' of covered entities signed) litigated for the right to run rebates; Second Sight (340B ESP and the Beacon pilot platform) is a BRG subsidiary, and BRG wrote PhRMA's Medicaid study.
ideas.solution: A charter owned by hospital associations and health-center networks, a data-use covenant barring audit use, a verdict API (eligible / duplicate / pay amount) for manufacturers, and a rebate-operations desk for small entities. Start with Medicaid and MFP verdicts, which need no rebates. Legal premise: the pilot was enjoined once (D. Maine, Dec 2025) and is challenged again (AHA, 9 Oct 2026); the House bill would pause rebates and the Senate bill would end the pilot, so the product must work with no rebates.
ideas.why_now: Pilot starts 1 Jan 2027 with 10 manufacturers (AbbVie, Amgen, Astellas, AstraZeneca, BMS, Boehringer, GSK, Merck, Pfizer, Teva); the Senate SUSTAIN bill wants an independent third-party clearinghouse contracted within a year of enactment; Cassidy's draft offers a claims-repository option; MFP duplicates loom.
ideas.wedge: Three state hospital associations or primary care associations as founding members, plus two manufacturers outside the approved ten.
ideas.path_to_100m: (a) Top 50 manufacturers x $1-3M for verdicts and settlement = $50-150M (my estimate; no public price); (b) 2,000 hospitals x $25k + 12,000 other covered entities x $3k = about $86M; (c) a statutory user fee, $50M base from FY2031 (secondary summary of the Senate draft). Total about $140-240M if it becomes the standard; needs about half the manufacturers and a third of covered entities. HEROIC SHARE, winner-take-most. Rebates alone: about $5.5B x 2.5% = $140M at 100% share, so the pilot cannot carry it.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Kalderos (Truzo; about 15 days to pay), Beacon and 340B ESP (Second Sight/BRG; 1,000+ entities submitting by 2022), Pillr (rebate readiness), Sentry, Wellpartner, Walgreens, Apexus.
ideas.why_they_lose: Neutrality: AHA members will not hand claims to a manufacturer-funded platform run by the pharma lobby's economist or by the plaintiff in the rebate case, and no hospital-side administrator will be trusted or paid by manufacturers.
ideas.moat: Network economies (two-sided: more covered entities means better verdicts for manufacturers) plus a cornered resource (the hospital-owned charter and any designation).
ideas.earned_secret: The impasse is about data use, not data existence. A firewall that returns only a verdict and a payment satisfies both sides' stated objection. (Hypothesis; test in 10 counsel interviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Draft the data-use covenant with hospital-side and manufacturer-side counsel; build the Medicaid and MFP verdict API on public and sample data; sign two state associations; open talks with two manufacturers outside the approved ten; monitor the AHA suit and Senate text.

ideas.title: Open TPA: 340B administrator with no pharmacy attached
ideas.one_liner: Flat per-claim pricing, a portable ledger so a hospital can leave CVS's or Walgreens' administrator without losing its positions, and an independent pharmacy network.
ideas.customer: Regional hospitals, FQHC networks and covered entities in states that protect contract pharmacies; independent pharmacies.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The covered entity's existing administrator-fee line; signed by the CFO or director of pharmacy.
ideas.problem: Fees track the drug price: Wellpartner's rises from 10% to 14% of the spread by year three and its 2023 TPA fees were $382M; Walgreens charges 8-20% of contracted reimbursement. Five chains/PBMs (Cigna, CVS, UnitedHealth, Walgreens, Walmart) hold 77% of 239,905 contract-pharmacy relationships; CVS told entities in Dec 2017 that Wellpartner would be the exclusive administrator for its pharmacies, and Sentry and RxStrategies sued (outcome unverified). A Senate draft would require flat fees per unit of service; Cassidy's draft would delink fees from price.
ideas.solution: Flat fee per claim, pharmacy-agnostic routing, neutral reporting, fee audit, and an exit service that moves virtual-inventory history. Legal premise: no law yet forces flat fees, so the product must win on price today.
ideas.why_now: Contract-pharmacy locations have fallen four years in a row to 31,593 (Rite Aid gone, chains closing stores); 19 states enacted 22 340B bills in 2025; federal fee-delinking bills are live; Apexus (the Prime Vendor) is under a Cassidy inquiry over its fees.
ideas.wedge: 5 FQHC networks and 5 regional hospitals in states with contract-pharmacy protection laws, with a 90-day price guarantee.
ideas.path_to_100m: $8 per claim (my estimate) x 12.5M claims = $100M. The national count of 340B pharmacy claims is not published (my estimate 100M +/- 50%), so that is 10-15% of claims, or roughly 25% of the chain-administrator fee pool. HEROIC SHARE.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Wellpartner (CVS), Walgreens 340B Complete, Sentry (Craneware), Pillr (bought Cooper Strategy June 2026), RxStrategies, Apexus (free tools).
ideas.why_they_lose: Chain administrators earn a percentage of the spread and steer to their own stores, so flat fees would cut their revenue; Sentry has no pharmacy leverage and is shrinking; Pillr is private-equity owned and sells through hospitals.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (note that a portable ledger lowers switching costs for everyone, including us).
ideas.earned_secret: The lock-in is the pharmacy-to-administrator tie, not the software, and the percentage fee rises with the drug price with no extra work.
ideas.first_90_days: Price against Wellpartner's published schedule; sign 3 independent-pharmacy groups; build the ledger export; run free fee audits for 10 prospects.

ideas.title: JG-Day for Payers: 340B cut pass-through desk for non-conflicted Medicare Advantage plans
ideas.one_liner: Give MA plans that do not own a 340B pharmacy business a contract-and-claims desk that uses CMS's new JG/TB/XX modifiers to pass the 340B cut through hospital contracts and audit modifier accuracy, paid a share of savings.
ideas.customer: MA plans and Medicaid MCOs outside the two conglomerates that sit in the five-chain list (UnitedHealth/Optum Rx and CVS/Aetna): Humana, Elevance, Centene, Molina, Blue plans, Kaiser (general knowledge on enrollment).
ideas.payer_and_signer: SVP provider contracting or chief payment-integrity officer; contingency 12-15% of savings (my estimate).
ideas.problem: From 1 Jan 2027 every OPPS drug line carries JG, TB or XX, the first verifiable 340B flag. MA contracts that reference OPPS rates may or may not pass the cut through; plans will try. Hospitals self-report the modifier and a JG costs them about 37%, so there is a standing incentive to report XX. Plans have no hospital-level 340B knowledge, and the two largest MA parents earn on 340B pharmacy spreads.
ideas.solution: Classify each hospital contract's drug language; propose amendments requiring the modifiers and audit rights; edit claims; score each hospital's 340B likelihood from OPAIS child-site registration, DSH status and HCPCS mix; audit XX lines; recover. Legal premise: MA contracts are private and federal law preempts most state rules on MA payment, but state 340B anti-discrimination laws (19 states enacted 22 340B bills in 2025) may reach hospital-administered drugs in commercial contracts; get counsel opinions state by state.
ideas.why_now: The modifier regime starts 1 Jan 2027; MA benchmarks lag FFS cuts so plan margins are squeezed first; the final rule is imminent.
ideas.wedge: Two mid-size MA plans, contract analysis for their top 20 340B hospitals, before the final rule.
ideas.path_to_100m: FFS 340B Part B payments are about $13B (derived in idea 2), so MA at 54/46 of enrollment is about $15B (my estimate). Full pass-through at 37% is $5.6B; 30% realized in two years = $1.7B; a 12-15% fee = $200-250M. $100M needs 40-50% of that pool, roughly the four largest non-conflicted plans. HEROIC SHARE.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Plan in-house contracting and payment-integrity vendors (Cotiviti, Zelis, Optum Payment Integrity; general knowledge, not searched). Molina, Moda and others already publish missing-modifier policies for 340B claims.
ideas.why_they_lose: Vendors owned by conglomerates will not police their parents' pharmacy profits; a modifier edit is a feature, not a service; none has a hospital-level 340B model.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against conglomerate-owned vendors plus a growing 340B-likelihood dataset.
ideas.earned_secret: The rate matters less than the audit right: the modifier is hospital-reported, so whoever can check it controls the savings.
ideas.first_90_days: Read 50 hospital-plan contracts for OPPS language; build the likelihood score from OPAIS and public cost reports; sign two plans on contingency; watch the final rule.

ideas.title: Specialty Door: shared specialty pharmacy utility for health systems
ideas.one_liner: A shared, accredited, PBM-credentialed specialty pharmacy that health systems use as their own front door (their patients, their 340B account, flat fee per script), timed to the Medicare any-willing-pharmacy rules arriving 2027-2029.
ideas.customer: The 40-60 health systems with the largest 340B specialty volume (specialty is 38.1% of units but 61.9% of 340B purchase dollars).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief pharmacy officer plus CFO; the budget is the contract-pharmacy and administrator fees they pay today (in Drug Channels' illustrative $5,000 specialty script, CVS's fee is $624 and Wellpartner's $497).
ideas.problem: Over 70% of health systems say their specialty pharmacy is frozen out by payers; limited-distribution drugs block about 30% of fill opportunity; one insurer wants two years of dispensing history and dual accreditation. So 340B specialty scripts flow to PBM-owned pharmacies that also charge the fees.
ideas.solution: One national entity with its own NPI, dual accreditation, network contracts and limited-distribution access, operating under each system's brand against the system's 340B account. Legal premise: the federal PBM reform signed 3 Feb 2026 includes Part D delinking and any-willing-pharmacy rules (effective 2028-2029 per one summary) and CMS is writing Part D pharmacy contracting standards; no commercial ownership ban was found.
ideas.why_now: PBM reform enacted; Rite Aid gone and chain store closures; manufacturers' single-pharmacy policies push entities toward in-house or designated pharmacies; contract-pharmacy locations down four straight years.
ideas.wedge: 3 systems with Medicare-heavy oncology and immunology volume; Part D first.
ideas.path_to_100m: The five chains earned nearly $3B gross profit from 340B in 2023 (likely $4B+ now, my extrapolation), about 5M high-value scripts at ~$900 each (my estimate). At $250 a script, 400,000 scripts = $100M, about 8% of chain volume or 10 systems x 40,000 scripts. Needs PBM networks to open, which only Medicare Part D will do by about 2029.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Trellis Rx (now CPS Solutions), Shields Health Solutions (Walgreens-owned), Pillr, PBM-owned CVS Specialty, Accredo and Optum Specialty, health-system in-house pharmacies.
ideas.why_they_lose: PBM pharmacies earn the fee they would have to give up; Shields belongs to a chain that is itself a contract pharmacy; Trellis builds one pharmacy per system and never aggregates network credentials.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in network credentials plus a cornered resource (accreditation and dispensing history).
ideas.earned_secret: 'Frozen out' is a contracting-entity problem, not a pharmacy problem: a shared entity clears volume thresholds no single hospital can.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 chief pharmacy officers; map each system's script volume by payer; line up a licensed, accredited acquisition target; read responses to CMS's pharmacy-contracting RFI.

ideas.title: Pigeonhole: IRA MFP-versus-340B duplicate-discount floor for manufacturers
ideas.one_liner: Using only data manufacturers already hold (340B chargebacks by ship-to pharmacy and the Medicare Transaction Facilitator feed), prove for each pharmacy and month the minimum number of units that received both MFP and 340B, and recover them.
ideas.customer: Manufacturers with selected drugs outside the approved rebate pilot (J&J, Novo Nordisk and Novartis are not in the 1 Oct list as reported by Becker's, which may not be exhaustive) and, from 2027, every manufacturer with a selected drug.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief pricing officer or VP government pricing and IRA operations; fee 10-15% of duplicates recovered or avoided (my estimate).
ideas.problem: The statute requires the lower of MFP or the 340B price but creates no process to stop both; CMS declined to prevent it; pharmacies cannot flag 340B claims (NCPA); HRSA's pilot is the workaround but covers 10 manufacturers; Walgreens routes all 2026 selected-drug Part D claims to MFP; a Health Affairs piece of 31 Jul 2026 (read only via search summary) says billions of duplicates are possible.
ideas.solution: For pharmacy P, drug N, month M take units bought on 340B accounts (A), units bought on non-340B accounts (B, from wholesaler transaction data) and units dispensed to MFP-eligible Part D patients (U, from the MTF feed). At least max(0, U - B) of the MFP units must have come from 340B stock. Example: if 60% of a pharmacy's units are 340B and 65% of scripts are Part D, at least 25% of units are duplicates. Output an evidence packet, a pharmacy attestation request and a recovery path. Legal premise: the MFP statute obliges manufacturers to pay refunds promptly, so unilateral withholding is risky; recover through consented offsets, CMS's dispute process, HRSA ADR or settlements, after a counsel opinion.
ideas.why_now: MFP started 1 Jan 2026 (10 drugs), adds 15 in 2027, 15 in 2028 including Part B, and 20 a year after (statute; general knowledge); the pilot excludes some manufacturers; the pilot may be enjoined again.
ideas.wedge: One non-pilot manufacturer's 2026 selected drug, 12 months of its 340B chargebacks and MTF data.
ideas.path_to_100m: HRSA's ~5.5% of 340B sales is about $5.5B at ceiling prices; assume 40% goes to Part D patients, giving about $2.2B of duplicates for 2026, growing with the 2027 list to $4-5B (my estimates). Recover 50%, fee 10-15% = $100-375M at 100% of manufacturers. Needs 30-40% share.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Kalderos (claims-level duplicate prevention; says Truzo can address MFP overlap), Beacon/340B ESP (BRG), the HRSA rebate pilot, CMS's MTF, manufacturers' in-house teams, IQVIA 340B analytics (general knowledge).
ideas.why_they_lose: Claims-level tools need covered-entity data, consent and months of integration; a lower bound needs none of it. Chargeback operations (trade) and IRA operations (government pricing) sit in different departments, so no one joins the two files.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (data licensing from manufacturers and wholesalers) plus process power.
ideas.earned_secret: Manufacturers already receive the two files that bound the problem; the pigeonhole argument needs no patient data. (Hypothesis; test on real files.)
ideas.first_90_days: Get a counsel opinion on recovery paths; license one manufacturer's chargeback and MTF files; run 12 months of the bound; brief the manufacturer's government-pricing head; compare against Kalderos output.

ideas.title: Clean Exit: sponsor-level cell captives built to be sold with the company
ideas.one_liner: A sponsored-captive platform for private-equity sponsors where every portfolio company gets a cell and every cell is born with its exit: buyer-ready accounting, a pre-priced loss portfolio transfer (LPT) at sale, and fund-level pooling above the cells.
ideas.customer: Middle-market PE sponsors with 10-50 U.S. portfolio companies; beachhead is healthcare services, dental, vet, behavioral and home-services platforms where workers' comp, professional liability, EPL and cyber are material. PitchBook counts about 13,300-13,500 U.S. PE-backed companies (March/June 2026, via Solomon Partners and WSJ).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The sponsor's operating partner or COO signs the program (insurance is an EBITDA lever the sponsor capitalises at exit); the fund CFO and GC clear related-party and LP-advisory-committee issues; each portfolio company's CFO opts in and pays premium from its insurance line.
ideas.problem: Brokers pitch sponsor captives with 25-50% savings (Horton Group, unverified) but adoption is thin. Proskauer lists the open questions for a captive covering separate portfolio companies as ownership, allocation of risk and return, financing and exits; Captive.com notes wind-down needs the regulator's assurance that no further claims will emerge; long-tail lines need 5-7 years of collateral. My inference (no source found): the buyer's quality-of-earnings team treats retained captive earnings as non-recurring and lenders treat collateral as debt-like, so the sponsor's CFO vetoes the captive at the sale.
ideas.solution: (1) Sponsored captive owned by the sponsor or a fund vehicle, one protected cell per portfolio company, fronted and reinsured above a set retention, cell collateral in a Treasury trust. (2) Exit package written at formation: transfer with the company to the buyer's program, novation of run-off to the sponsor's core cell at an actuarial price, or a pre-priced LPT/adverse-development cover from a legacy partner under a rate card. (3) QoE kit: independent-actuary market-equivalent premiums, profits recognised in the core, standard buyer data-room page. (4) Fund-level pooling above cells so 30-50 companies diversify each other. Legal premise to verify (not verified): tax treatment of related-but-separate insureds (risk shifting/distribution, deductibility), domicile rules for sponsored captives with unrelated participants, LP agreement limits on related-party fees.
ideas.why_now: The tail-versus-hold mismatch has just closed: average U.S. PE hold about 7 years in 2025 versus about 6 in 2021, about a third of 13,325 unsold companies held 7+ years, and exits below $1B enterprise value are down about 28% since 2021 (Solomon Partners citing PitchBook), so sponsors need operating levers. Woodruff Sawyer's 2026 outlook lists portfolio-style programs gaining momentum; the UK PRA/FCA captive consultations (CP11/26, CP26/29, closed 2026-10-14) put captives in front of sponsors' lawyers.
ideas.wedge: Two or three sponsors with 15-30 healthcare-services or home-services platforms each; 30-40 cells in year 1 (WC, PL/EPL, cyber, auto) at about $1.5M average premium = $45-60M of premium.
ideas.path_to_100m: Pool (my assumption, no source found for PE-portco insurance spend): 13,400 PE-backed companies x about $1.5M annual insurance spend (about 1% of a $150M-revenue company) = about $20B premium. Fee stack of 6-7% of premium (captive management/actuarial, reinsurance placement override, legacy structuring fee, tech). $100M needs about $1.5-1.6B premium = roughly 1,000 portfolio companies (about 7-8% of the universe and of the premium pool) across 35-50 sponsors at 20-30 cells each. Share is not heroic; the sales cycle is. Year 6-7.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Brokers and captive managers sell sponsor captives case by case (Horton Group, Captive.com articles, Proskauer commentary). I found no dedicated sponsor-level facility or exit protocol from Marsh, Aon or Alliant in 2025-26 (searched; 'none found', not 'none exist'). Insurance collateral funding providers pitch liquidity to PE. Legacy buyers (Enstar and peers, from memory) do large transfers but do not offer exit options up front. UK regime not live until mid-2027.
ideas.why_they_lose: Brokers are paid on placements and annual renewals, and a captive with a built-in exit removes recurring brokerage; large captive managers price bespoke work for large clients; legacy buyers prefer big bespoke deals; nobody on the insurance side controls the sale process, while a sponsor-aligned platform with deal counsel, a QoE playbook and committed LPT capacity covers the part the sponsor CFO actually fears.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (standard documents and equity accounts across 30-50 cells under one core); process power (an exit playbook accepted by QoE firms and lenders); cornered resource (pre-committed legacy capacity).
ideas.earned_secret: Captives do not fail at formation; they fail at the sale. Buyers' accountants read retained earnings as non-recurring and nobody wants a five-year tail, so the CFO quietly vetoes the captive the broker sold. Fix the exit and the savings brokers promise become bankable.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview three sponsor COOs and three QoE leads on how captive profits and collateral were treated in real sales. Pull five-year loss runs for 20 portfolio companies and run a cell-level feasibility. Sound out three legacy buyers for a rate card on sub-$25M reserves. Draft cell documents and the buyer data-room page. Get a tax and fund-document opinion before any pitch.

ideas.title: The 12th Member: a cross-agency fill-rate machine for group captives
ideas.one_liner: A neutral network that assembles new group captives from pre-scored members spread across hundreds of independent agencies, because the scarce input is the twelfth qualified, similar member in the room.
ideas.customer: Independent agencies (producers of record) and mid-market firms with $0.25-5M of casualty premium in industries too thin in any one agent's book to form a group. Captive Resources (CR) estimates about 70,000 potential casualty members versus 6,500 served, and about 200,000 potential medical stop-loss clients versus about 10,000 served.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Company CFO or owner (premium moves from a carrier to the captive; the fee sits inside that spend); the agency principal (flat fee plus profit share); the captive board.
ideas.problem: A group needs homogeneity and critical mass: practitioner sources say 6-12 qualified insureds and $5M+ of premium at inception (2004 article); Utah's regulator says at least $1M of annual premium. Each group is sponsored by one agency and filled from its book, so thin niches never form. Large consolidators earn carrier profit-sharing (my recollection, unverified) and have no reason to steer clients out; Marsh/Aon/Gallagher serve large clients; CR is capacity-bound as a consultant (50+ groups over decades).
ideas.solution: (1) Free 'captive fit' engine: five years of loss runs, payroll/class codes, FMCSA/OSHA records, telematics where available, scored against group benchmarks. (2) Anonymous cross-agency ledger of prospects by class, size, geography. (3) Syndicate builder composes 10-15 alike members, runs actuarial feasibility and sets terms. (4) Turnkey group captive on shared infrastructure (cells, front, reinsurance, TPA) or paid placement into an existing group. (5) Agency stays producer of record on a flat-fee schedule plus profit share. Legal premise to verify: domicile licensing for group captives, producer-compensation disclosure, securities treatment of membership interests.
ideas.why_now: Casualty is still hard: Marsh Q2 2026 shows casualty +7% and umbrella/excess +15% (risk-adjusted) while overall U.S. commercial fell 2%; WTW says over a quarter of lead umbrella programs were restructured. Luzern Risk's $45M Series B (Sept 2026) shows capital is arriving for middle-market captives but Luzern is a captive manager, not a member assembler. CR projects group captive premium to $10B by 2030 from $6.5B.
ideas.wedge: Twenty-five independent agencies in one vertical (regional food/beverage distributors, propane/fuel distributors, landscape and snow, specialty contractors); three syndicates of 12 members = about $40-50M of premium.
ideas.path_to_100m: Fee stack 4-5% of premium (formation, sponsor/program fee, share of management). Needs about $2.2B of premium: roughly 2,000 members at $1.1M average (assumption), about 150 syndicates of 13, about 3% of CR's 70,000-prospect estimate. HEROIC if the market does not grow: $2.2B is about 22% of 2030 group premium ($10B); it only works if the network creates groups that would not otherwise exist (the roughly 63,500 unserved casualty prospects). Sources: Travelers exec ($6.5B), CR ($5.5B, 70,000 prospects, $10B by 2030).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Captive Resources (consultant to agency sponsors, 6,500 casualty members, 97-98% retention), Roundstone, Strategic Risk Solutions, Marsh (Fleet Solutions Insurance Ltd. for transportation), Aon, Gallagher/Artex, Travelers Captive Solutions, Hylant's group captive services (MSL), Reliance Partners (transportation), Luzern Risk (digital captive manager). None found that assembles members across agencies (searched; 'none found').
ideas.why_they_lose: Every group is bound to its sponsor agency's book and consultants are paid by sponsors, so no one is paid to move a prospect across sponsors; consolidators have a contingent-commission conflict; Marsh/Aon cost to serve is too high for $500K accounts; Luzern runs captives but does not fill them.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more agencies fill groups faster, attracting more agencies); data asset (admission scoring from loss runs across hundreds of agencies); switching costs once a group exists.
ideas.earned_secret: Capital and fronting are not the bottleneck; the twelfth qualified, similar member is. Every agent knows 40 good prospects and can name three of the twelve needed, but the other nine sit in other agents' books where nobody can see them.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit 25 independent agencies in one niche; collect 200 loss-run packages under NDA; build and back-test the fit score against known group results; pick one niche and sign a sponsor for the first syndicate; line up a captive manager, front and reinsurer as vendors.

ideas.title: Zero-Collateral Cell Reinsurer: a pooled $250M reinsurer that qualifies for the U.S. no-collateral rule
ideas.one_liner: A Bermuda multi-cell reinsurer capitalised above $250M by hundreds of captives plus institutional money, so every group captive that is one of its cells cedes from U.S. fronts without regulatory collateral.
ideas.customer: Group captives (casualty and MSL), mid-size fronted single-parent captives and rent-a-captive cells, and their sponsor agencies; fronting carriers are the counterparty.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Group captive board chair and member CFOs with the sponsor's captive manager; budget line is the cost of collateral (LOC fees of 25-100 bps plus carrying cost of cash/trust assets) and the fronting fee. The fronting carrier's chief underwriting officer signs the reinsurance.
ideas.problem: Fronts usually require 125-150% of the projected loss fund as collateral, sometimes with a 20-75% buffer, set 'at the sole discretion of the fronting company' and reviewed annually; release takes 3-7 years after policy expiry on long-tail lines (Captive.com, Captive International, Business Insurance; several sources dated 2005-2024). Regulation requires some collateral because a small captive is an unauthorised reinsurer; the front adds the rest. An older source quotes fronting fees of 6-10% of premium. No individual captive can reach the $250M no-collateral threshold.
ideas.solution: (1) Bermuda segregated-accounts or Class 3A-type reinsurer capitalised with $250M+ (member surplus, surplus notes, insurance-asset-manager/ILS capital). (2) Each captive is a cell with its own loss fund and risk-sharing; the platform's general capital backs fronts for cell default (a credit-enhancement fee replaces collateral). (3) Lead-state approval then NAIC passport as a reciprocal-jurisdiction reinsurer; AM Best rating (Aug 2025 criteria opened a path to rate incorporated cells) to meet A- VII contract/lender requirements. (4) Revenue: capacity fee about 1.5-2% of premium (below members' estimated net collateral carrying cost of 2-4% of premium; my assumption), cell management about 2.5-3%, share of investment income. Legal premise to verify (this is the whole business): whether general-account capital counts toward each cell's cessions, whether new reinsurers face seasoning/old-liability collateral rules, whether fronts will cede without contractual collateral, passport mechanics.
ideas.why_now: NAIC's 2019 amendments created the reciprocal-jurisdiction reinsurer: $250M minimum capital, zero collateral; Bermuda, Japan, Switzerland listed from 2020-01-01; all 56 NAIC jurisdictions adopted by 2022; lead-state approval passports via the NAIC. Fronting is the squeezed link: MGAs/insurtechs compete with captives for paper (Concert CEO), AM Best flags offshore/unauthorised/unrated reinsurers, five fronts exited or de-emphasised, Conning sees a softening market; the Aug 2026 CICR is asking whether insurance securities can replace excess cash collateral. Why not here yet: the framework is six years old and built for large reinsurers, the threshold is unreachable for any single captive, sponsors are agencies not balance sheets, and fronts like the discretion.
ideas.wedge: Convert 6-10 existing group captives from two sponsor agencies ($400-600M premium) into cells; capital $60-80M from members plus about $170M third-party.
ideas.path_to_100m: Revenue about 5% of premium all-in (assumption) means about $2B of cell premium. That is about 20% of 2030 group captive premium ($10B, CR projection) or about 10% of a broader $20B pool of fronted group, MSL and mid-size captive premium (my assumption). HEROIC on the narrow pool; plausible only if widened to MSL and mid-size single-parent captives. Needs at least $250M of capital and carries real tail risk if cells fail.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Traditional fronts (Old Republic, Sompo, Zurich, from memory) demand collateral at their discretion. Concert Group (A-, $100M raise) and PRP Performa are captive-focused fronts with friendlier terms, not collateral-free. Marsh's Mangrove cell facility (cells +14% by number, +47% by premium in 2025), Gallagher/Artex and Aon cell programs lack a $250M balance sheet. Large RJ reinsurers (Swiss Re, Munich Re, from memory) do not write small first-loss cells. None found pooling captives into one RJ-qualified reinsurer (searched; 'none found').
ideas.why_they_lose: A front cannot waive collateral without taking unsecured credit risk on small captives, and it earns from the discretion; AM Best penalises unsecured recoverables. Broker cell facilities cannot raise $250M of risk capital from members they also place business for. CR is a consultant, not a risk-bearer.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (capital efficiency); cornered resource (RJ approval plus rating); switching costs (cells hold members' equity); counter-positioning (fronts cannot copy without giving up collateral spread).
ideas.earned_secret: Collateral is a negotiating lever, not a risk measure: regulation sets a floor and the front adds the rest at its sole discretion. The $250M threshold turns the question from 'how much will this $20M captive post?' into 'is the pool a reinsurer?', which no individual captive can answer and a pool can.
ideas.first_90_days: Retain Bermuda and U.S. counsel for a written view on cells under the RJ test; pre-consult a lead state and the BMA; get term-sheet-level responses from two fronts (including Concert and PRP) on ceding to a pooled RJ reinsurer with no collateral; model capital and the guarantee fee; sign LOIs with 8 group captives and their sponsors.

ideas.title: The 97% Book: buy the agencies and managers that sponsor group captives
ideas.one_liner: A permanent-capital holding company that acquires the agencies, consultants and independent managers that sponsor and run casualty and MSL group captives, the one corner of commercial insurance with 97-98% retention and member-owned capital accounts that make leaving costly.
ideas.customer: Sellers: founders of sponsor agencies, consultants and independent captive managers (revenue $8-30M each). Revenue payers: group-captive member boards that sign multi-year management and program agreements.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Revenue is paid by group-captive member boards (multi-year management/program agreements). The buyer's signer is the platform investment committee; each captive board must consent to assignment of the management agreement.
ideas.problem: Group-captive sponsor and manager fees are hidden inside agencies and valued like ordinary commission revenue; owners age; members worry about continuity and key people. Big consolidators are buying captive managers (Howden bought ARM Group in 2024, Holmes Murphy bought Global Captive Management, Davies bought Citadel Risk, Aon bought Nordic Mutual) but their retail agencies conflict with captives.
ideas.solution: Acquire in sequence (i) sponsor agencies with 3-8 groups, (ii) independent captive managers and MSL specialists, (iii) group-captive TPA units. Consolidate reinsurance/front purchasing, back office and reporting; write a covenant that the owner never sells members commercial insurance; cross-launch new groups through the combined sponsor network. No AI required; automation helps margin but is not the thesis.
ideas.why_now: Group premium is growing about 11% a year to $10B by 2030 on CR's projection; retention is 97-98% versus high-80s/low-90s market-wide; strategics paying for captive managers set comparables; PE capital wants recurring revenue. Why not here yet: the assets are private, relationship-based and tied to a consultant (CR) whose cooperation is needed, and the consolidators that could buy them sell commercial insurance to the same clients.
ideas.wedge: First deal: a $15-30M-revenue sponsor agency or consultancy with 5+ groups; about $100M of platform equity; 8-12 deals over five years at $8-15M of revenue each.
ideas.path_to_100m: Sponsor and manager fee pool of 7-9% of premium (assumption; CR members pay professional fees rather than commissions): $455-585M on $6.5B today, $700-900M on $10B in 2030. $100M is about 11-14% of the 2030 pool via 8-12 acquisitions plus about 10% organic growth. Enterprise value about $400M at 4x revenue; funding $300-500M of equity and debt. A financial-engineering path more than a product path: credible, late-cycle, dependent on key people staying.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Marsh, Aon, Gallagher/Artex and WTW run groups and managers; Howden/ARM, Holmes Murphy/GCM, Davies/Citadel consolidate managers; CR is family-held and private; PE-backed brokers (Hub, USI, Acrisure, from memory) buy commission books. No platform buying group-captive sponsors as a category found (searched once; 'none found').
ideas.why_they_lose: Boards will not approve assignment to a buyer that sells their members commercial insurance, which rules out the large brokers; the no-cross-sell covenant is the counter-position. Sponsors who want independence prefer a partner with permanent capital and no cross-selling.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (members leave their equity behind for 4-5 years after exit); scale economies in reinsurance and front panels; brand with member boards.
ideas.earned_secret: Group-captive revenue is the stickiest in commercial insurance, yet it is valued as ordinary agency commission revenue. The arbitrage is the multiple and the retention, not technology.
ideas.first_90_days: Map the 90+ casualty and 50+ MSL groups (sponsor, consultant, manager, premium, fee schedule); call 20 sponsors and get three LOIs; read three management agreements for assignment and key-person clauses; line up a $50M anchor equity commitment and a debt partner.

ideas.title: Pareto TPA: paid on the 7% of claims that carry 40% of the cost
ideas.one_liner: A claims administrator for owner-managed casualty programs that puts its best adjusters, nurses and defence strategists on the top slice of claims by dollar exposure and is paid a share of verified savings against the captive actuary's pick.
ideas.customer: Group-captive boards and sponsor agencies, large single-parent captives, and large-deductible or self-insured workers' comp and liability programs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Risk manager or captive board claims committee; budget is the TPA/ALAE/ULAE line paid from the loss fund.
ideas.problem: NCCI data show a tiny fraction of claims drives much of the cost: claims of $100K-$500K were 7.3% of claims and 41.3% of costs (2004-06 study, dated); claims above $1M were under 0.5% of lost-time claims but up to 15% of costs; fast-emerging large claims were 59% of $1M+ claims in 2023 versus 27% in 2003. TPAs staff by claim count and bill per file or hour, so the best people are not on the claims that matter.
ideas.solution: (1) Top-decile desk takes over a claim at triggers (reserve above $50K, attorney involvement, surgery, ICU, venue). (2) LLM file review for missing records, causation, litigation budgets and settlement valuation against an outcomes database built across programs; senior humans decide. (3) Fees: small base fee on desk claims plus 15-25% of verified savings against the actuary's expected ultimate. (4) Run as the owner's representative alongside the current TPA, which keeps the small-claim tail. Legal premise to verify: state adjuster/TPA licensing and any rules on compensation tied to claim outcomes (structure as consultant to the captive, not adjuster of record); front's claims-control clauses.
ideas.why_now: Models can read ten-year claim files; nuclear-verdict severity makes the top slice matter more; captive claims committees control claims by design. CLARA Analytics launched an agentic AI claims workforce for complex casualty and Veltha (YC S26, tiny seed) is an AI-native WC TPA, but both sell productivity to carriers and TPAs, not savings-share to owners.
ideas.wedge: Five group captives (trucking, construction) with $30-100M of premium each hand over open top-decile claims for a 12-month fee-on-savings pilot.
ideas.path_to_100m: Effective revenue about 5.6% of claim dollars under management (4% base plus 20% of an assumed 8% saving). $100M needs about $1.8B of top-decile claim dollars under management. Assumptions: Marsh-managed captives' $79.1B premium at a 55% loss ratio = about $43B of losses, half long-tail ($21.5B), top slice 45% = about $9.7B a year; group captives add about $1.75B (60% loss ratio on $6.5B, top slice 45%). That is about 15% of the captive casualty top slice, or 5-7% if large-deductible and self-insured programs (not sized) are as large. HEROIC on captives alone; savings attribution is a standing dispute risk.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Sedgwick, Gallagher Bassett, Crawford, CorVel, ESIS (Chubb), Optum (all per-claim or per-hour); AI claims vendors CLARA ($60M raised in total), Five Sigma ($24M), Agentech ($3M seed), Veltha. Litigation-management and claim-audit boutiques (from memory). None found selling savings-share on the top decile to owners (searched; 'none found').
ideas.why_they_lose: Per-claim fees and carrier customers who buy speed make outcome fees a pay cut for the TPA, automating adjuster hours cuts its own billable base, and a savings-share invites audits of its reserving; fronts that bundle claims earn on volume.
ideas.moat: Process power (playbooks per injury class and venue); data asset (settlement outcomes across programs, which no single captive has); switching costs on open claims.
ideas.earned_secret: Claims are staffed by count and cost is by dollars. About 7% of claims make about 41% of the cost and the fee schedule pays the same for every file, so nobody puts the best adjuster on the 7%.
ideas.first_90_days: Pilot with one captive manager and two groups: review 200 open claims; fix the savings baseline as the actuary's inception pick; build the outcomes database; get a licensing opinion on outcome-linked fees.

ideas.title: Retained-Risk Bureau: the NCCI of captives, self-insureds and large deductibles
ideas.one_liner: A member-governed data cooperative that pools loss triangles, claim outcomes and safety data from captives, TPAs and self-insured programs and sells development patterns and proof of selection to reinsurers, carriers and MGAs.
ideas.customer: Buyers: reinsurers, excess carriers, MGAs, fronts. Contributors and subscribers: captive managers, TPAs, sponsor agencies, captive boards.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Head of casualty reinsurance underwriting or chief actuary (external data and analytics budget); MGA founders; sponsors' CEOs for member-facing tiers.
ideas.problem: ISO and NCCI collect statistical data on insured business; the retained layers (captives, self-insured, large deductible) are invisible to everyone. Advocates say captives outperform but I found no rigorous independent study: '15-30% lower premiums' comes from brokers and managers, and AM Best's recent view is that captive results came under pressure in workers' comp and RRG commercial auto. Excess reinsurers therefore price off market loss costs plus an uncertainty load, and captives lack a neutral benchmark for collateral release or treaty renewals.
ideas.solution: (1) Give-to-get data charter with anonymisation, run by a neutral operator; LLM extraction from loss runs and bordereaux. (2) Products: captive loss-development factors by line/class/size (for collateral and reserve talks); a selection-effect index (how group-captive members perform versus insured-market expectation); admission scores for sponsors; TPA benchmarks; API for reinsurers and MGAs. (3) Over time an advisory loss-cost product that reinsurers cite in treaties. Legal premise to verify: antitrust on information exchange (neutral aggregator with safeguards), data ownership between captive, front and TPA, HIPAA for MSL data (non-PHI only), McCarran-Ferguson treatment of statistical agents.
ideas.why_now: Group-captive premium of $6.5B and third-party captives of $4.4B (Marsh) now produce enough data; Conning finds fronting programs' early loss ratios have developed adversely seven years running, so reported data are under suspicion; reinsurers are pushing fronts to retain more; data bureaus' pricing power is visible (Verisk underwriting segment $569M of Q2 2026 revenue per a secondary source).
ideas.wedge: One segment where data are richest: trucking auto liability and workers' comp in group captives. Ten groups contribute; deliver a selection-effect report to two reinsurers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Mature revenue (assumptions): 40 reinsurers at $300K-$1.5M ($30M); 150 excess carriers/MGAs at $100-400K ($30M); 2,500 captives, sponsors and managers at $15-40K ($60M); 20 fronts at $250K ($5M) = about $125M. $100M is roughly 4% of the underwriting-analytics spend Verisk's segment implies (about $2.3B a year, secondary source). Adoption assumptions are HEROIC; contributions and trust take years.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Verisk/ISO and NCCI (insured-market statistics); AM Best captive composites (dated); Marsh, Aon, Gallagher/Artex benchmarking (client-only); Milliman, Pinnacle and other actuaries (bespoke); NAIC annual-statement data for RRGs (free); Luzern and Huscarl will accumulate data as proprietary advantage. No neutral cross-captive bureau found (searched; 'none found').
ideas.why_they_lose: ISO and NCCI answer to carriers and receive data from insurers, not captive owners, and carriers gain from opacity about the retained world. Brokers' benchmarks are sales tools tied to their own clients. Managers hold data but will not hand it to competitors.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more contributors, better factors, more value); cornered resource (contractual data rights); switching costs once embedded in collateral talks and treaty pricing.
ideas.earned_secret: Everyone says captives outperform and nobody can prove it, because the data live in 8,000 sets of spreadsheets and front bordereaux. Whoever can prove it, or disprove it, sets the price of every excess layer and every collateral-release schedule.
ideas.first_90_days: Draft the charter and antitrust review; get five managers or TPAs to share anonymised triangles for 50 programs; compute a first selection-effect result for trucking; show it to two reinsurers and ask for a price.

ideas.title: Broker Mutual: a member-owned liability RRG that underwrites every freight load
ideas.one_liner: A risk retention group owned by mid-size freight brokers and 3PLs that insures negligent-selection claims after Montgomery and prices each tendered load on the carrier, truck and driver behind it.
ideas.customer: U.S. freight brokers and 3PLs ranked roughly 40th to 1,000th by gross revenue ($50M to $2B) plus asset-light agent-network brokerages; not the top 25 (C.H. Robinson carries $135M of auto liability limits above a $10M per-claim deductible).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The broker's CFO or owner. Budget: contingent auto liability, third-party liability and E&O; TIA's president puts a brokerage's total insurance at 1-3% of revenue and says the figure he hears most is a 5x increase. TIA board endorsement helps distribution.
ideas.problem: On 2026-05-14 the Supreme Court held 9-0 that negligent-selection claims against brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA. The only federal broker financial requirement is a $75,000 surety bond. TD Cowen: about 10 underwriters write broker auto liability, expected to fall to eight (two exits already); a top-10 broker's liability premium roughly tripled; a large broker's excess above a $15M primary went from $3M to $10M; few brokers carry above $100M outside the largest; the Lipe verdict against C.H. Robinson was reported at $600M in late July. About 22,000-28,000 brokers exist and the top 100 hold 84% of the market. The federal carrier minimum is still $750,000 against a $36M median trucking nuclear verdict (ATRI, as reported).
ideas.solution: (1) Vermont-domiciled RRG: under the Liability Risk Retention Act one state licence lets an RRG write liability (not workers' comp) nationwide for owner-insureds in similar business; A-rated reinsurance tower with excess for large losses. (2) Per-load underwriting: member TMS sends each tender to the RRG API; the RRG scores the carrier (authority age, safety rating, inspections, crash history, live insurance verification, identity and double-brokering flags) and truck/driver data where available; premium = base plus per-load charge; high-risk loads priced up or blocked. (3) Immutable selection file per load as evidence of standard of care in discovery. (4) Dividends in good years; GL/E&O/cargo fronted via a partner. (5) Year 3+: shared balance sheet with the zero-collateral reinsurer for an excess mutual covering the top 100 and carriers. Legal premise to verify: contingent auto is 'liability' under 15 U.S.C. 3901, member-ownership/similar-exposure tests, multistate registration delays, Vermont Act 77 (effective 2026-07-01) limits on RRG loans/investments to members, shipper contracts demanding A-rated insurers (launch behind a fronted or rated layer).
ideas.why_now: The ruling is five months old; the FMCSA broker financial responsibility rule took full effect 2026-01-16; underwriters expect to price carrier selection and ask for vetting records (Higginbotham, Lockton, FreightWaves); reinsurer appetite for the class has fallen (TD Cowen). Proof a captive can be a profit centre in a contractor network: Landstar's insurance segment earned about $26M of revenue and $10M of operating income in Q1 2025 (about $15M external).
ideas.wedge: Twelve to fifteen founding brokers ($100M-$800M gross revenue) with documented vetting who have been quoted 2-3x; $15-25M of initial capital pooled from members plus a surplus-note investor; TIA endorsement; first-year premium $20-30M.
ideas.path_to_100m: Tier of about 900 brokers outside the top 100 with $50M+ gross revenue (assumption). Average member: $300M gross revenue at about 13% net revenue = $39M net revenue; TIA's 1-3% implies $0.4-1.2M of insurance; after repricing about $0.9M for liability (assumption). 110 members x $0.9M = about $100M of premium, about 12% of that tier's roughly $800M pool. REVENUE HERE IS INSURANCE PREMIUM; fee-only revenue (manager/program/tech at 12-15%) would be $12-15M. Year 5+ option: carriers on the approved list buy primary auto liability via the RRG (2,000 carriers x $30K = $60M, assumption).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Marsh BrokerSafe (Aug 2025: A-rated panel up to $5M primary plus $5M London excess, with analytics); Falvey (Accelerant paper, $1M/$2M primaries); TIA-endorsed Avalon program; Reliance Partners and TCB Insurance Programs (non-admitted); Higginbotham transportation division (31 staff, Oct 2026); USA Risk Group reportedly seeking a Delaware transportation RRG (undated source); Aon Small Fleet Advantage RRG (directory listing only). Big brokers self-insure (C.H. Robinson; Landstar's captive). Carrier-vetting software (Highway, MyCarrierPackets, Carrier Assure, from memory) feeds underwriting but bears no risk. No broker-owned RRG found (searched; 'none found').
ideas.why_they_lose: Marsh's facility is placed capacity: Marsh does not own the underwriting result, cannot hold members to a tendering standard and sees only annual submissions. The shrinking pool of about 10 underwriters prices on revenue and loss history, not per-load selection. Members who own the dividend have a reason to vet better.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against annual-submission underwriting; switching costs (TMS integration plus evidence file plus member equity); cornered resource (cross-broker carrier-selection data); later network effects as the RRG's carrier list becomes the market's approved list.
ideas.earned_secret: After Montgomery a claim is decided in discovery by one question: what did you know about this carrier when you tendered the load? Underwriters and plaintiffs ask it from the same eight data points. Whoever holds the time-stamped selection file can price the risk and defend it, so the record is the product, and it can only be built inside the TMS.
