ideas.first_90_days: Get LOIs from TIA and 12 brokers; retain counsel for an LRRA and Vermont opinion and a Vermont RRG manager; collect loss runs and TMS exports; build the load-scoring model from FMCSA bulk data and test on historic loads with known claims; get soft quotes from Lloyd's and Bermuda reinsurers; file the business plan and a $15-25M capital term sheet.

ideas.title: The TPA Captive: stop-loss captives sponsored by the people who see the claims first
ideas.one_liner: Give independent third-party administrators their own medical stop-loss group captive in a box, so employers with 50-1,500 lives stop buying lasers and annual repricing from carriers who see the same claims six to twelve months later.
ideas.customer: Independent TPAs (about 4,300 once, now hundreds after consolidation, per a Cognizant/TriZetto piece), each administering 50-500 self-funded employers, and those employers. KFF 2025 (as reported): 67% of covered workers are in self-funded plans, 27% at small firms.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Employer CFO or head of HR (benefits budget; stop-loss premiums up 12.7% on average for 2026 in Segal's 225-plan data); the TPA CEO co-signs (retention and differentiation versus carrier ASO bundles).
ideas.problem: Segal 2026 data (via actuary.info): stop-loss premiums +12.7%; $1M+ claimants grew about 25% a year for four plan years (2.44x since 2022); carriers laser beyond oncology/transplant and add gene-therapy exclusions; median medical trend 9%; GLP-1 allowed PMPM for covering employers rose from $2.41 to $22.59 (2022-24); employers raise specific deductibles from $150K to $250K+, pushing variance into the aggregate layer. Stop-loss premium was $35.5B in 2023 (Oliver Wyman). CR serves about 10,000 MSL members of about 200,000 potential and calls MSL a real target.
ideas.solution: (1) Platform lets each TPA sponsor a cell or its own group captive: front, reinsurance panel, captive manager, actuary, collateral trust, investments, employer onboarding. (2) The TPA's live claims feed (prior authorisations, case-management flags, large-claim alerts, Rx) drives underwriting continuously, enabling 'no new lasers', multi-year rate corridors and a pooled catastrophic layer. (3) Employer retains first $100-250K per person, captive pools the next layer, reinsurers take above $1M. (4) TPA earns admin fees plus a 3-5% sponsor share; the platform earns about 6.5% (management about 2%, reinsurance override about 2%, underwriting/tech about 2%, other 0.5%; assumption). Legal premise to verify: state stop-loss rules for small groups (minimum attachment points), ERISA/MEWA status, tax treatment of captive-funded stop-loss (one source says the IRS has not definitively addressed it); target employers of 50+ lives.
ideas.why_now: The structural break above; carriers adding gene-therapy exclusions; employers dropping GLP-1 coverage (6% of 500+ employers for 2026) while Lilly Employer Connect (launched 2026-03-05, Zepbound KwikPen $449 per dose as reported) and Novo's Waltz Health and 9amHealth programs (Jan 2026) open direct-to-employer drug channels that TPAs can plug into.
ideas.wedge: Ten independent TPAs with 100+ groups each and renewal pain; start with groups of 100-1,000 lives and a two-year rate corridor; first 100 employers at about $400K of stop-loss premium = $40M.
ideas.path_to_100m: About $1.5B of stop-loss premium in TPA-sponsored captives at 6.5% = about $98M: 80 TPAs x 40 groups x $470K. That is about 3,200 employers (1.6% of CR's 200,000 prospects, a third of CR's 10,000 served) and about 3% of an estimated $45B stop-loss market in 2026 (my extrapolation from $35.5B in 2023). Not heroic on share; strong captive-consultant competition is the constraint.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Captive Resources (50+ groups, MSL a stated target), Strategic Risk Solutions' MSL Captive Solutions, RMC (fronting/reinsurance facility for captive managers and MGAs), Sun Life, QBE and Skyward Specialty's AH Captive Solutions (carrier-run group stop-loss programmes), Hylant GCS, Roundstone, Zenith Risk Strategies (small MGU), Yuzu Health (General Catalyst-backed TPA infrastructure for small employers, per a newsletter headline; unverified), Aradigm (gene-therapy pooling, May 2026 Quantum Health deal). Carrier-affiliated TPAs (Meritain/Aetna, Cigna, UnitedHealthcare) hold large shares. None found giving independent TPAs a captive platform (searched; 'none found').
ideas.why_they_lose: Stop-loss carriers see claims through TPA submissions with a lag, reprice annually and laser: that is their profit lever, and they sell ASO bundles that compete with independent TPAs. Benefit brokers earn commissions on stop-loss and cannot recommend a captive that removes them. CR's model is built around agency and consultant sponsors, not around the party that holds the claims feed.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (live claims data from many TPAs); switching costs (employer equity accounts in the captive, 97-98% retention in CR's groups); scale economies in reinsurance.
ideas.earned_secret: The stop-loss carrier is the last person in the room to learn about a $1M claimant; the TPA knew at prior authorisation, months earlier. Adverse selection is a data-latency tax the employer pays, and whoever owns the claim feed can underwrite without it.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit five independent TPAs through their associations and sign data-sharing agreements; back-test three years of claims on 20 groups against actual stop-loss premiums and lasers; choose a domicile with MSL experience and sign a front and a reinsurer for the $1M+ layer; get an ERISA, state stop-loss and tax opinion.

verdicts.title: Zero-Down Copper Exit: pay for the cutover out of the phone bill

competitors_found.name: MarketSpark
competitors_found.what_they_do: Managed POTS replacement for large multi-site enterprises: site surveys, install, cloud management, 24/7 support, alarm and elevator lines. Retail case study audited ~360 locations and installed 350 kits.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $7M Series B (Apr 2021, led by IDT); says it supports 35 Fortune 500 companies; 'tens of thousands of lines' per its own case study

competitors_found.name: Ooma AirDial
competitors_found.what_they_do: Cellular/IP POTS replacement for fire panels, elevators, alarms; sold via 41 resellers incl. T-Mobile for Business, AireSpring, Carahsoft; Frost & Sullivan 2026 leader.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Public company, FY27 revenue guide $332-333.5M; AirDial services revenue +75% YoY; stated long-term goal 300k lines / $100M ARR (not yet reached)

competitors_found.name: Alarm.com Fire Communicator (ADC-FC100)
competitors_found.what_they_do: UL 864 dual-path broadband/LTE commercial fire communicator replacing POTS on existing panels; launched 2026-07-16 through service-provider partners and distributors.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Alarm.com is a large public company with an installed dealer channel

competitors_found.name: DataRemote POTS IN A BOX
competitors_found.what_they_do: Appliance plus flat managed cellular plan for fire, burglar and elevator lines.

competitors_found.name: TPx Digital POTS / EPIC iO / 5Gstore
competitors_found.what_they_do: Managed alarm-line replacement; EPIC iO advertises $0 CapEx options and single consolidated bill for multi-location; 5Gstore rents hardware plus service at $69.99/month.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Carrier/MSP and reseller scale; no disclosed figures

verdicts.substitutes: Owner's alarm dealer converts its own monitored base with Telguard/NAPCO StarLink/Alarm.com cellular communicators at roughly $15-40/month versus $50-120 per POTS line; integrators with national accounts (Everon, JCI, Convergint) do this for chains; telecom carriers sell their own replacements; owners can simply keep paying the POTS line while copper lasts.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 110k sites x $900 = $99M checks arithmetically, but the share is not credible: Ooma, a public company with 41 resellers, lists $100M ARR / 300k lines (about $333 per line per year) as a long-term goal it has not hit. The first AT&T wave is about 90,000 customers in 18 mostly rural states; FCC switched lines fell from 27.2M (mid-2022) to 15.0M (June 2025), so the pool is a shrinking one-time wave. A $75/site price leaves little saving to share against $15-40 cellular communicators, and financing $110-175M of deployments is unproven (alarm lenders lend on UL-monitored RMR, not found for communicator-only data contracts). Realistic: $20-30M ARR.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Premise 'no owner-side, financed, brand-neutral program found' is false (MarketSpark). Pool file's FCC source DOC-419252A1 is the circulated draft FCC-CIRC 2603-03; adoption of FCC 26-19 on 2026-03-26 confirmed only via secondary sources. The order text never names fire alarms or elevators; the link is from vendors. NFPA 72 allows a single supervised UL 864 cellular path subject to AHJ acceptance and edition.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real mandate and budget line, but the owner-side managed program is already sold by MarketSpark, Ooma and Alarm.com; the $100M needs more than the leader's own stated goal.

verdicts.title: Wire-Center Sweeps: convert every unconverted small system in a retiring footprint, one visit each

competitors_found.name: Local alarm dealers and roll-ups (Pye-Barker, Everon and peers)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Convert their own monitored accounts to cellular communicators during service visits; the monitoring dealer already holds the customer and the panel.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Thousands of dealers; Pye-Barker 57 acquisitions in 2025 per pool file

competitors_found.name: Ooma AirDial resellers incl. POTSTracker lead tool
competitors_found.what_they_do: Inbound lead generation and resale of AirDial to businesses.

competitors_found.name: MarketSpark
competitors_found.what_they_do: Site-by-site POTS replacement with local surveys.

verdicts.substitutes: The owner's existing alarm/monitoring dealer; a $300-600 communicator swap folded into a routine service call; do nothing until the carrier notice arrives.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $48M install plus $59M RMR in year 4 needs 40k conversions a year at 15%+ close rate from cold canvass; the idea itself calls that heroic (8-16% of assumed endpoints). The premise of '800-1,500 businesses per approved wire center in a metro' contradicts the evidence: AT&T's latest approved batch (the 'additional 25% of wire centers') covers only about 90,000 customers in 18 states, mostly rural, with effect from 2026-11-15; Ooma's management says Verizon is not yet active. Originated contracts sold at about 1x revenue ($540/yr) cannot repay a $1,200 swap plus door-to-door CAC.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Wire-center calendar premise holds directionally (retirement is wire-center by wire-center, 90-day notice) but the early waves are tiny and rural; the timing conflict the idea notes (June 2026 vs a year later) is unresolved by any primary source found.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Demand arrives in small rural pockets and is already served by the monitoring dealer; cold-canvass CAC for a commodity swap cannot support a $100M path.

verdicts.title: Second-Opinion Desk: free quote checks that become the owner's neutral fire-and-life-safety program

competitors_found.name: Telgian
competitors_found.what_they_do: Founded 1985; centralized multi-location fire and life-safety program management (inventory, ITM, capital replacement, budgeting, portal), markets itself as unbiased and separating inspection from repair.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Serves 'tens of thousands of facilities'; third-party estimates $80-111M revenue, ~360 employees (https://growjo.com/company/Telgian); ownership unresolved

competitors_found.name: The Compliance Engine (Brycer)
competitors_found.what_they_do: AHJ-side reporting network for fire inspection reports; some jurisdictions mandate it.

competitors_found.name: ServiceTrade / Inspect Point / Ember
competitors_found.what_they_do: Contractor-side software that turns deficiencies into repair quotes (the opposite side of the table).
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Ember $10M (8VC, Menlo); Inspect Point $28M (Mainsail); ServiceTrade 1,300+ contractors per idea

verdicts.substitutes: JLL, CBRE and Cushman integrated facilities management; owners' own bid rounds and public RFPs; NFPA 72 (2022) 7.5.7.1.1 reportedly already entitles owners to software access and passwords (forum summary, unverified); consulting engineers (Jensen Hughes).
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $100M of principal revenue at $2.5-4k per site is 25-40k sites (the 1.5M-site pool is an unsourced assumption), but at 20-25% gross margin it is only $20-25M of gross profit; the free quote checker produces no revenue. Telgian's ~$80-111M after 40 years is the observed ceiling of this model. Cintas Fire's 50.8% Q4 FY26 gross margin is confirmed (SEC 8-K), which supports the conflict-of-interest story but not a bigger neutral player.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: No legal premise issue; the 'no neutral owner-side player' claim is false because Telgian exists.
verdicts.deciding_reason: A 40-year-old independent incumbent (Telgian) shows the model tops out near $100M of revenue, and the entrant would be thin-margin pass-through.

verdicts.title: Panel Liberation: zero-down replacement of locked proprietary fire panels

competitors_found.name: Every fire contractor and OEM dealer (JCI/Simplex, Honeywell/Notifier, Siemens, Carrier/Edwards)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Panel replacements routinely bid and awarded, e.g. CSULB ~$8M Simplex-to-Notifier CM@R; Valencia College $786,896 for end-of-life panels.

competitors_found.name: Open-protocol manufacturers (Fire-Lite, Silent Knight, Notifier)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Sold as multi-dealer serviceable panels; Notifier says owners can change service provider at any time.

verdicts.substitutes: Owner demands passwords and programming files from the installer (NFPA 72 2022 7.5.7.1.1 per secondary summary); competitive bids on open panels already; Siemens partners can take over any Siemens panel per technicians; right-to-repair legislation proposals.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $20k average x 5,000 replacements = $100M, but '60-80k panel replacements a year' has no source and vendor guides put panels at $5k-$25k+; no fire-alarm lease-purchase or zero-down program was found, and public owners face appropriation limits on multi-year pay-from-savings deals. It is a construction contractor margin business with no network, data or software moat; after three years the $45-60M recurring estimate depends on winning ITM bids against the lock-in holders.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Lock is real mainly for Simplex (a SUNY Stony Brook sole-source cited that only JCI was qualified), not Notifier or Siemens; owner software-access right under NFPA 72 2022 is unverified against the code text.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Lock-in is narrow (mostly Simplex), the work is ordinary bid-out capital construction, and there is no scalable moat.

verdicts.title: Full-Service Fire Protection: one flat price per square foot a year, repairs included

competitors_found.name: Johnson Controls Comprehensive Service Offer and Enhanced Service tier
competitors_found.what_they_do: Preventive and corrective maintenance of JCI and third-party systems; Enhanced tier covers system labor and optional panel parts; a 2026 school proposal priced semi-annual test plus labor plus panel parts at $3,566 for one panel.

competitors_found.name: SimplexGrinnell 'Full Service Contract' (public K-12)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Five-year full-service agreement with Pasco County Schools, ~$710k/year, with some repairs still billable.

competitors_found.name: Cintas Fire Protection
competitors_found.what_they_do: Route-based inspection and repair; segment gross margin 50.8% in Q4 FY26, organic growth 10.7%.

verdicts.substitutes: Time-and-materials repair on multi-award bids with hourly rates and parts markups; public specs that already ask for monitoring, parts and labor, inspections in one annual price; owners self-insuring repair budgets.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Price per square foot is about 2-3x too high: $0.30/sf over ~96B sf of US commercial floorspace (CBECS 2018) is $29B, above IBISWorld's entire $22.1B industry; the pool file's $8-12B recurring spend implies $0.08-0.15/sf, so a 50k sf building is $4-7.5k, not $15k. At $0.10/sf, $100M is ~20k buildings (3-5% of an unsourced 400-600k), and gross margin must hold at 30%+ with no loss history and adverse selection.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Insurance-reclassification risk is lower than feared: the NAIC Service Contracts Model Act exempts maintenance agreements, commercial transactions and sales to non-consumers, though state versions vary (verify per state).
verdicts.deciding_reason: Flat-fee comprehensive fire service is already sold (JCI, public full-service specs), and the revenue per building is overstated by 2-3x.

competitors_found.name: BlackStarTech FireSight
competitors_found.what_they_do: Robotic remote fire watch; first product certified under FM 3270 (March 2025), scoped to hot work and temporary outages.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Co-developed with Fike; funding not found

No US impairment-event count exists in any source found. Memberships at $15-40/month duplicate services the insurer and dealer provide free, and per-event revenue is guard-hours the idea says it will cannibalize.

competitors_found.what_they_do: Fire/life-safety and specialty contractor; record backlog above $5B in Q2 2026; data centers expected 10-12% of 2026 revenue; aims to convert projects to recurring ITM.

competitors_found.what_they_do: MEP prime with data-center-driven growth; names labor as its primary constraint.

competitors_found.what_they_do: Design-build fire detection, pre-action, clean agent and commissioning for data centers.

result.pool_note: A mandated shock (copper exit) and a capex boom (data centers) left no venture-scale gap. Every layer has a funded owner: MarketSpark, Ooma and Alarm.com for the box; Telgian for the neutral program; Brycer for AHJ data; APi and Comfort for data-center labor. verdicts.revenue_math_check: The pitch assumes $0.9M of liability premium per $300M-gross member. Albrecht puts a $30-40M-gross broker at $10K rising to $30-40K, which scales to about $0.3-0.4M at $300M, and TD Cowen says a 3PL spends about 10 cents of insurance per $1 a carrier spends. 110 members is then about $35-45M of premium; $100M needs 250-330 members, 25-35% of the assumed tier. Year-one premium from 12-15 founding brokers is about $5-8M, not $20-30M. Fee-only revenue at 12-15% is $4-7M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport (2026-05-14, unanimous) confirmed. RRGs cannot join state guaranty funds (15 U.S.C. 3902), trucking RRGs have failed (Spirit $199M unpaid, Global Hawk), and many shipper contracts require rated insurers. Vermont RRG loan/investment limits effective 2026-07-01 per a trade report. TIA 1-3% of revenue figure not traced to a primary.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Best shock in the pool but the premium pool is about 3x smaller than assumed, Marsh already supplies rated paper, and an unrated RRG carries verdict tail on thin capital.

verdicts.substitutes: Existing MSL captives run by brokers and consultants (TPA-agnostic), carrier stop-loss with multi-year rate guarantees, level-funded products.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 80 TPAs x 40 groups x $470K is $1.5B. Milliman's 2019 survey put captive coverage under 10% of stop-loss premium; even at 15% of the $45B market (about $6.8B, my assumption) the idea needs about 22% of all MSL captive premium through a channel with no precedent. Reinsurers (RGA, Zurich, Swiss Re) stepped back in 2026.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: State stop-loss minimum attachment points, ERISA/MEWA status and captive tax treatment unverified. No TPA found that sponsors its own captive; a Vermont regulator slide flags appearance of insurance when a TPA is state-regulated insurer.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real pricing pain (Segal +12.7%) but crowded with consultants and carriers, no TPA appetite for insurance risk evidenced, and tightening reinsurance capacity.

result.pool_note: Captive pool is large but the fee layer is concentrated: Captive Resources advises roughly 85% of group-captive premium, PE-backed consolidators already buy managers, and open heterogeneous groups fill thin niches. Ideas needing double-digit share or a regulatory loophole (RJ status excludes captive classes) failed. The freight-broker shock is real but its premium pool is small.
